title: iOS 27.3 beta 2 is out now, adding face unlock to iPhone Duo and AI limits
content:
Macworld





Apple has begun beta testing for iOS and iPadOS 27.3, along with the 27.3 versions of all its other operating systems. This release should bring early Apple Intelligence features to China, as well as the Audio Intelligence features of Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, the redesigned Health app, and new Siri AI features within apps.
We expect the final public release will take place sometime near the end of November or early December.
Updated November 16: The second beta of iOS 27.3 is out now. It adds a face unlock option to iPhone Duo and Apple Intelligence limits, along with video podcasts in the Apple TV app.
What’s new in the iOS 27.3 beta
Here are some of the new features and changes discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta so far:
Apple Intelligence limits: When using cloud-based Apple Intelligence features, users are subject to an unspecified number of daily uses. This applies to Siri AI, Clean Up / Extend / Spatial Reframing in Photos, Image Playground, and third-party apps that use Apple’s cloud AI models. If you have an iCloud+ plan, you get higher limits, from 2x for the 200GB plan up to 20x for the 12TB plan.
Siri AI “Ask About Page”: Siri AI can already read and react to whatever is currently on your iPhone’s screen, across any app. There is a new “Ask About Page” Siri AI feature in iOS 27.3 that allows it to read an entire web page to answer your query.
iPhone Duo face unlock: A new option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode allows you to unlock your iPhone Duo using facial recognition. This only works for unlocking your phone, not for entering passwords or making payments, and it requires you to have recently used Touch ID or a passcode to unlock your phone. You’ll have to first go through a sort of “Face ID lite” setup similar to what you do on HomeView. 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Close to Lock iPhone Duo: A new option in Settings > Display & Brightness called Close to Lock will lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.
Video Podcasts in Apple TV app: The Apple TV app will show video podcasts, and they sync with your progress in the Podcasts app. On a related note, Macworld now has its video podcasts in Apple Podcasts (and Apple TV). Check it out.
New Health app: The newly-designed Health app is back, after a brief appearance in the 27.2 betas. 
Audio Intelligence: Together with an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, the Live Rewind and Siri Recap features are now available. Read more about privacy with these features here.
Safari features: Safari gets vertical tabs, Siri AI actions, and adaptive dark mode. Read more about these feautres here.
Siri AI languages: Siri AI expands to Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.
iPhone Duo Reachability: An accessibility feature made to shift content to the side on the iPhone Duo, so it’s easier to reach on the extra-wide phone.
Apple Intelligence in China: China gets some basic Apple Intelligence features like Writing Tools, Visual Intelligence, Clean Up, Genmoji, and more. Siri AI is not available.
Fitness+ Gym Strength: New features in Fitness+ to build a gym strength training plan including the ability to track reps and weight.
StandBy updates: On regular iPhones, StandBy mode has more of the options and configurability found on iPhone Duo. It still only works when your iPhone is charging, unlike iPhone Duo.
Siri actions in Apple apps: Siri gets a lot of new capabilites across Apple apps like Calendar, Music, Messages, Reminders, Weather, and more. You can ask Siri what it can do in each app.
Siri actions in third-party apps: The 27.3 developer previews add App Intents for developers that allow them to integrate their content and actions into Siri. So data from third-party apps can be part of your “personal context” and you can use natural language to have Siri perform actions in those apps (once they are updated to do so).
iOS 27.3: How to install
If you want to test the iOS 27 beta releases but are not a registered developer, follow these steps:
Click Sign Up on the Apple Beta page and register with your Apple ID.
Log in to the Beta Software Program.
Click Enroll your iOS device.
Open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update.
In the Beta Updates section, select the iOS Public Beta.
It may take a few moments after registering for the beta option to appear in Software Update.
iOS 27.3: How to install the developer beta
You’ll need to be registered as an Apple developer, but a free developer account will do. You can get one via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app:
Download the Apple Developer App from the App Store.
Open the app.
Tap on Account.
Sign in using your usual Apple ID.
Find out everything you need to know about iOS 27 in our iOS 27 superguide.

content:
The second beta of iOS 27.3 includes a new "Ask About Page" feature for Siri AI. 


‌Siri‌ can see the entire content of a webpage, including content that isn't currently in view on the screen. If you're looking at a website with a long menu, for example, you can ask ‌Siri‌ to surface all of the options that are gluten-free. Or if you're getting ready for a trip, you can ask ‌Siri‌ to read through a long guide and put together a packing list based on what's on the page. 

Right now, ‌Siri‌ has on-screen intelligence, but it relies on what's in view. Access to a full webpage will make ‌Siri‌ more useful for summarizing content. 

Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather.

In Mail, for example, ‌Siri‌ can unsubscribe you from mailing lists and undo recently sent messages. In Weather, ‌Siri‌ can add locations to your weather list, or control weather notifications. In Files, ‌Siri‌ can organize content, delete files you haven't accessed for a set period of time, and more.

title: ‘Worst Apple launch ever’? HomeView issues pile up as early adopters slam new smart hub
content:
Macworld





HomeView went on sale just three days ago, but the product has already been deluged with complaints. While the hardware has been well received, some owners have reported a variety of software issues across multiple threads on multiple forums. These cover areas as diverse as Music, Photos, device setup, Siri performance and screen auto-brightness.
On the MacRumors forums, we found four separate threads discussing HomeView’s shortcomings, with some 170 posts at the time of writing. The shortest of these focuses on Siri and the Music app, complaining that the device “won’t stop music that is playing,” advising the user that something has gone wrong and to try again later, and that it won’t restart music that’s been paused. A second thread reports that Siri simply won’t play music. One respondent to this adds the further complication: “when I ask it to play music, continue music, skip tracks etc, despite talking very clearly to the HomeView (Siri clearly on screen listening) it does the action on my iPhone.”
Another thread complains that Siri on the HomeView can’t set timers. (This might seem somewhat trivial, but it’s actually a key function because the HomeView has been marketed as a useful tool in the kitchen.) Many other forum users confirm they’ve also experienced this, and the thread author claims this is backed up by a call to Apple support.
The longest thread on that forum has a total of 129 posts at present, and begins with a broad complaint about “problem after problem.”
“I have two HomeViews, and they simply don’t work properly,” the author begins with obvious exasperation. “One unit spent half of yesterday saying it was downloading Siri. Once Siri sort of started working, it wouldn’t do basic things like set timers because ‘the software update on this device doesn’t support that.’ The Photos app on the main screen shows a photo from my phone and advertises a collection of favorites, yet when I tap it, the HomeView says Photos aren’t supported on this device. My second HomeView had all these exact same problems.
“This morning, the first one suddenly works for setting timers, though it still won’t do anything with Photos. The second one showed the Siri bubble this morning, but wouldn’t even respond to anything I asked. A reboot got Siri responding again, still without timer support. I rebooted it again, and now it won’t even show the Siri bubble, just repeating ‘downloading Siri’ (again) any time I use the wake word.”

				
					

				
			
HomeView’s early adopters have complained about vaious software issues with the device.

Foundry




Reports of issues aren’t by any means confined to the MacRumors forums. On Reddit we discovered another four threads with similar complaints. We’ve seen widgets forgetting user preferences and needing to be reset; auto-brightness failing to do anything until you turn it off and on again; music libraries and playlists being difficult to access; and the device refusing to pair with an iPhone, resulting in failed setup.
In most of those cases, to avoid boring the reader, I’ve cherrypicked a single complaint out of several that are discussed. But there are hundreds of complaints about dozens of separate issues. And that’s even without the usual contributions of Apple Support Community, a frequent destination for users reporting issues of this nature which was conveniently shuttered by Apple last week.
To an extent it’s to be expected that a brand-new product will have software problems in the first few days after launch; when the product is a company’s first attempt at a new market, as is the case here, we should expect even more of them. Many of the issues, we would hope, will be solved by software updates; and in some of the threads you’ll see positive outcomes when users received help that actually worked. (One was advised that the problem might be caused by them running a beta version of iOS. When they factory-reset the device, the problem went away.) This isn’t totally surprising, nor will all of these problems be an issue in the medium and long term.
Nevertheless, even by the standards of new tech products, this is a lot of complaints covering a lot of ground. Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, but the company needs to address this as a matter of urgency.
creator: Macworld

title: iOS 27.3 Beta Adds Daily Siri AI Limits and iCloud+ Upgrades
content:
With the latest iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 betas, Apple is starting to test limits and paid upgrades for Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features.


Every Apple device gets a free daily access allowance for Siri AI and ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features that rely on server-side AI processing, such as Image Playground and Clean Up in Photos. When that limit is hit, there will be an option to extend usage with an iCloud+ plan. Everyday ‌Siri‌ commands will always remain free, but here's what will be limited:

 	
‌Siri‌ AI for multi-step, personal context requests that rely on server-side processing, such as asking ‌Siri‌ what time you need to leave from home to make it to a location on time.

 	
Image generation and editing tools, including ‌Image Playground‌ and the AI options in ‌Photos‌ like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing.

 	
Workflows and automations in Shortcuts that rely on AFM Cloud and AFM Cloud Pro.

 	
Third-party apps that use Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute for AI features.


"Everyday" ‌Siri‌ commands include those with a single ask, such as "set a timer for 30 minutes" or "text Eric I'm on my way." It's the more complex, multi-step requests that count against limits.

Apple's existing ‌iCloud‌+ plans will include higher daily usage for ‌Siri‌ AI and ‌Apple Intelligence‌, with no change in pricing. If you already subscribe to an eligible ‌iCloud‌+ plan, you will have higher usage limits. Free limits are per device, not per account, and do not roll over. 

More access starts with the 200GB ‌iCloud‌+ plan, which is priced at $2.99 per month. Users who subscribe to this plan have up to a 2x usage limit. Users who subscribe to the $9.99/month 2TB plan get up to 5x usage. The $29.99/month 6TB plan comes with up to 10x usage, and the $59.99/month 12TB plan offers up to 20x usage. Family members who share a plan will have a shared usage pool.

 	
50GB - No limit increase

 	
200GB - Up to 2x limit

 	
2TB - Up to 5x limit

 	
6TB - Up to 10x limit

 	
12TB - Up to 20x limit


Every Apple device will use the free daily limit first, and when that's reached, ‌Siri‌ AI and ‌Apple Intelligence‌ will use the ‌iCloud‌+ paid access. In a family group, a device that hits the free limit will start drawing from the shared pool on a first-come, first-served basis. Limits will reset at around 12:00 a.m. in the user's current time zone, and in families, the reset is based on the plan purchaser's time zone.

Each of the four categories has a different limit, and Apple will likely use the beta testing period to refine those limits and make sure people aren't hitting their caps too quickly. Limits depend on feature category, request complexity, and system demand, and they could change over time. 

Apple plans to give warnings when people are approaching their limits, and a notification when the limit has been hit. From there, users will be able to purchase additional access through an ‌iCloud‌+ plan, or wait for their limit to reset.

title: Latest macOS beta: What’s new and should you install it?
content:
Macworld





Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. The latest update, macOS 27.2, became publicly available on October 26, completing its beta cycle. 
The newest beta is macOS 27.3. The developer beta became available on November 3, 2026. The public beta became available a few days later. Developer beta 2 was released on November 16, 2026.
Beta releases give developers and testers early access to upcoming features, fixes and refinements. However, unfinished software can introduce bugs, compatibility problems and increased battery drain, so we recommend caution – particularly if you rely on your Mac for work.
This guide tracks developer and public beta availability, explains what’s new, and helps you decide whether to participate. You’ll also find installation instructions, advice on reducing the risks, and guidance on returning to a public release.


What’s the latest macOS beta? 
Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.
Latest developer beta: macOS 27.3 beta 2, released November 16, 2026.
Latest public beta: macOS 27.3 public beta 1, released November 5, 2026.
Previous beta cycle: macOS 27.3 beta 1, released November 3, 2026.
macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.

What’s new in the latest beta?

				
					

				
			
New features in macOS 27.

Foundry




Apple began testing macOS 27.3 with developers on November 3, 2026, and public beta testers on November 5. Changes being tested include the following Safari updates:
Vertical tabs: Open tabs can appear in a sidebar rather than across the top of the browser window.
Adaptive Dark Mode: Safari can apply a dark appearance to websites that don’t offer their own dark mode.
Siri browser controls: On compatible Macs, you can ask Siri AI to organize tabs or clear Safari’s cache.
Apple has also opened a developer preview that lets third-party apps connect their content and actions to Siri AI. This should eventually allow Siri to carry out more tasks in supported apps, but availability will depend on developers adding support and Apple’s rollout.
Further additions are planned, although they have not been confirmed for this beta:
Additional Siri AI languages: Apple says support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese is coming soon.
Broader Siri awareness in Safari: Apple plans to extend Siri’s understanding of webpage content beyond what is currently visible.
Automatic password changes also remain a promised feature, but their inclusion in macOS 27.3 has not been confirmed.
Separately, Apple released Xcode 27.3 beta, its app-development software, on November 3, 2026.
The 27.3 beta includes a major change to Full Disk Access (FDA). Users will need to make the extra effort to allow an app to have FDA. Learn more.
Features may change during testing. We’ll update this section as more changes are discovered.
See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta. 


						

							


Should you install the macOS beta?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.
Install if…
You need to test apps
You want early access to new features
You have a secondary Mac available
Wait if…
This is your primary work machine
You rely on niche or specialist software
Stability is critical to your workflow


						

							






Who are you Should you install?

A developer testing appsConsider the developer beta
An enthusiast with a spare MacConsider the public beta 
General user with one MacStay on macOS 27

 






What are the risks of installing beta software?
Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.
System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.


						

							


Safety precautions and best practices
If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:
Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.


						

							


How to install the macOS beta

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds. 
The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.
You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.
To install the beta follow these steps:
Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues. 
Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
Enable Beta Updates.
The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.
As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.
Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.


						

							


How to get a free Apple developer account
If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:
Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
Open the app on your iPhone. 
Tap on Account. 
Tap on Sign In. 
Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 
If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Who can run the macOS beta?
Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.
Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.
In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below. 
If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.





2.
macOS public beta vs developer beta
Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).
Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).
There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement
Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install. 
The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 
If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.





3.
Is the macOS beta stable?
By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 
If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:
We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.
We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.





4.
How to prepare your Mac for the beta
Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.
Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!
Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.





5.
How to send feedback to Apple
Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.
You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.
It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.
If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.





6.
Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?
Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.  





7.
Can I talk about the beta publicly?
According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”
However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.





8.
How to downgrade from the macOS beta
You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.
Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.





9.
Is the beta free to download? 
Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.





10.
Can I go back to the stable version?
Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.
If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.





11.
Should I install the beta on my main Mac?
Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.





12.
Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?
You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.





13.
How often are new beta versions released?
New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.





14.
Is the macOS beta safe to install?
The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.





15.
Will my apps work with the macOS beta?
Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

title: Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness
content:
Some owners of Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display say they experience eye strain, headaches, and dizziness when using the laptop, with affected users pointing to the screen's brightness-control system as a possible explanation.


A significant number of complaints have appeared on Reddit, X, and the MacRumors forums since the new models launched earlier this month. The discussions on MacRumors include a dedicated PWM thread, a separate owner poll, and comments in the reviews and display-details threads.

one user said trying the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ in an Apple Store for around 30 minutes left them with a severe headache. The user said they had previously struggled with OLED screens before finding newer implementations tolerable, and called for an option to change the Mac's dimming behavior.

Reddit user described how reading text, especially against a black background, brought on dizziness and nausea. They said their ‌OLED‌ iPad Pro did not produce the same symptoms. In the main MacRumors forum thread, a 16-inch PROLED owner reported a headache and mild nausea that began to ease after switching back to a mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌. Another member, posting in the separate poll thread, said they were returning their PROLED laptop for similar reasons after previously having no difficulty with ‌OLED‌ devices.

The suspected issue is pulse width modulation (PWM). An ‌OLED‌ screen produces light through its individual pixels. With PWM dimming, the display changes the time spent at brighter and darker levels during a rapidly repeating cycle. Spending less time at the brighter level reduces the average amount of light reaching the viewer, making the screen look dimmer. 

Those fluctuations can occur too quickly to look like an obvious flashing screen, but some people report discomfort with displays that use them. PWM frequency describes how often the brightness cycle repeats. It is different from refresh rate, which is how often the displayed image updates, so a 120Hz ProMotion specification does not tell you the screen's PWM frequency.

Notebookcheck's testing of the 14-inch PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ recorded 240Hz flickering whenever brightness was set to 99% or lower, with a measured amplitude of 56%. In other words, the light output fluctuated 240 times per second, and the amplitude describes the size of those fluctuations. The publication warned that sensitive users could experience eye strain or headaches due to the specification.

Mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌ displays also use brightness modulation, but Notebookcheck measured a much higher frequency of 14,880Hz on the 14-inch M4 Pro model. Such rapid fluctuations are generally less likely to cause discomfort for PWM-sensitive users.

Display Pulse Smoothing accessibility option on supported iPhones. The setting offers another way to dim the ‌OLED‌ screen at low brightness, although Apple cautions that it can affect display performance under some conditions. macOS does not offer an equivalent control, but Apple could add one in the future. 

OLED MacBook Pro models start at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch version. Apple continues to sell the mini-LED models alongside them.

title: Early Black Friday deal knocks AirPods Pro 3 to $179
content:
Macworld





		
Apple AirPods Pro 3
View Deal
AirPods Pro 3 have been on shelves for a while, but they’re still the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy, especially when you can get them on sale. While they can regularly be found for around $200, Amazon is selling them for $179 in this early Black Friday sale. That’s a $69 discount from its $250 MSRP and no far off its best price ever.
Apple says the AirPods Pro 3 remove twice as much unwanted noise as the previous model, which we were able to hear in our review. What we liked most, however, was just how comfortable and securely they fit into ears, which was something we complained about with the Pro 2. The ear tips now come in five sizes so it’s easier to find a snug and secure seal. Adaptive EQ helps tune the sound further, making adjustments based on the shape of your ear and how the earbuds fit. And of course, AirPods Pro 3 are built to deliver the impeccable sound you expect from Apple’s high-end earbids, with fuller bass and clearer details comapred to the 2nd-gen model.
Battery life is also something we loved when we reviewed these buds; we gave them a 4.5-star rating. You get up to 8 hours of listening with noise cancellation on or up to 10 hours in Transparency mode. That’s a full workday. And if you’re working out, a built-in heart rate sensing tracks your heart rate and calories burned across 50 workout types. If you don’t like wearing an Apple Watch when working out, these buds will bridge that data gap.
So don’t wait till next week and go get this early Black Friday deal on the Apple AirPods Pro 3 before it runs out.

title: iPad 2027: Release date rumors, price and A18/A19 upgrades
content:
Macworld





Apple’s next entry-level iPad may not be the flashiest iPad update of 2027, but it could be one of the most important. The affordable model is reportedly set to receive a faster chip that will finally bring support for Apple Intelligence.
The current iPad, released in March 2025, remains a capable tablet for students, families and everyday users, but it is now the only iPad in Apple’s lineup that doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. A new model expected in early 2027 should address that limitation, potentially with an A18 or A19 chip.
Other changes are expected to be relatively modest, with Apple likely to retain the current design and LCD display while focusing on performance and connectivity improvements.
Here’s everything we know so far about the 2027 iPad, including its expected release date, price, design, chip and other specs.
What’s new vs 2025 iPad A16: At a glance


2027 iPad predictions2025 iPad

Launch dateEarly 2027March 2025
Processor A18 (maybe A19) A16 
RAM8GB (rumored)6GB
Wi-Fi  Wi-Fi 7 Wi-Fi 6
Bluetooth Bluetooth 6Bluetooth 5.3
Apple IntelligenceYesNo
DesignUnchangedUnchanged

 






2027 iPad release date: When will Apple launch the next entry-level iPad?
First half of 2027 launch predicted
Apple’s next entry-level iPad is expected to arrive in the first half of 2027, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. As outlined in our November 2 report, Gurman expects Apple to announce updates to the standard iPad, iPad Air, and iPad Pro during that period.
Earlier reporting suggested the entry-level model could arrive as early as the first quarter of 2027, followed by updates to the iPad Air, iPad Pro, and Apple Pencil in the spring. The latest forecast gives a broader window extending through June, but a January-to-March launch still remains possible.
The timing has shifted from an earlier forecast that placed the new entry-level iPad in the iOS 26.4 release window back in May 2026. The reasons why Apple did not introduce a replacement during that period remain unclear. Chip availability and software readiness may have influenced its plans.
Should you wait? 
Unless you can find a really good deal on the current-generation iPad, we recommend waiting for the 2027 iPad if you’re considering an upgrade. The next-generation iPad is expected to deliver a meaningful upgrade with a faster chip, more RAM, and support for Apple Intelligence, making it a much more future-proof choice.


						

							


2027 iPad chip: Will the new iPad use the A18 or A19 chip?
A18 or A19 chip expected
6-core CPU and 5-core GPU likely
N1 chip for improved Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
The next iPad is expected to use either the A18 or A19 chip, with conflicting evidence pointing to both possibilities. Macworld has seen internal Apple code specifically linking the new J581 and J582 models to the A19, while Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in March 2026 that Apple had prepared an A18-powered model. It’s possible Apple has tested multiple configurations or subsequently changed its plans.
The A18, which debuted in the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus in 2024, would be a substantial upgrade over the A16 in the current iPad. Crucially, it would also bring the 8GB of RAM needed to support Apple Intelligence.
However, there is strong evidence for the A19 as well. As we reported in December 2025, leaked Apple code linked the J581 and J582 iPad models to the A19 chip used in the iPhone 17.
Until further information emerges, either chip remains plausible. Reports of A18 Pro shortages, linked to demand for the MacBook Neo, shouldn’t necessarily affect supplies of the standard A18.
What to expect
A18 chip: Features a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU in the iPhone 16. Apple could use the same configuration or a binned version in the iPad. It should provide a substantial performance increase over the A16, while 8GB of RAM would enable Apple Intelligence.
A19 chip: Also features a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU in the iPhone 17. If Apple uses it, the A19 would offer a larger performance upgrade over the A16 while likewise providing the memory required for Apple Intelligence.
Other specs
We have seen internal-code that indicates the new iPad will contain Apple’s N1 wireless chip. First introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup, the N1 handles Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Thread connectivity. Its inclusion could bring Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.x, upgrading the current iPad’s Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3.
For cellular models, Apple will likely use its in-house C1 modem (or a variant of it), continuing its shift away from third-party suppliers while improving efficiency and integration.


						

							


Why does Apple Intelligence matter for the iPad? 
Apple Intelligence introduces a range of AI-powered features designed to enhance creativity, productivity, and real-time communication, including:
Image Generation: Tools like Image Playground and Genmoji allow users to create custom visuals and personalized emojis from text prompts.
Live Translation: Integrated into FaceTime and Messages, this feature provides real-time translated captions during calls, effectively giving every user a personal translator.
Photo Editing: The “Clean Up” tool uses AI to identify and remove unwanted background objects from photos, a task that previously required complex manual editing.
Writing Tools: System-wide rewriting, proofreading, and summarization in apps such as Mail and Notes. 
Smart Shortcuts: Automation of repetitive tasks using intelligent actions and text summarization. 
Priority Management: AI-driven Priority Notifications and Priority Inbox to surface time-sensitive information.
These features require at least 8GB of RAM and a more powerful Neural Engine, which means Apple Intelligence is currently limited to M-series iPads (Air and Pro) and the A17 Pro iPad mini.
By contrast, the standard iPad with the A16 chip (released in March 2025) does not support Apple Intelligence. This is a notable limitation for long-term value, especially as future versions of iPadOS are expected to rely increasingly on AI-driven features.


						

							


2027 iPad display: No OLED or ProMotion
11-inch Liquid Retina LCD expected
No OLED upgrade expected
60Hz refresh rate expected, without ProMotion
The next entry-level iPad is expected to retain an LCD screen. Although the iPad mini gained OLED in late 2026 and the iPad Pro already offers it, there is no indication that the next standard iPad will receive the same upgrade.
We expect a display matching the current A16 model: an 11-inch Liquid Retina screen with a resolution of 2360 by 1640 pixels, 500 nits of brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate.


						

							


2027 iPad design: No new design

				
					

				
			
Apple currently offers the iPad in four colors.

Apple




The next entry-level iPad is also expected to have the same dimensions: 9.79 x 7.07 x 0.28 inches (248.6 x 179.5 x 7 millimeters) and weigh 1.05 pounds (477 grams). 
We haven’t heard anything about new colors, but since Apple hasn’t changed the color palette (blue, pink, yellow, silver) since its original release, it’s possible we get a couple of new options.


						

							


2027 iPad cameras: Will Apple update the FaceTime camera?

				
					

				
			
Britta O’Boyle





12MP rear camera 
12MP Center Stage front camera 
The current iPad has two 12MP cameras, with the front ‘FaceTime’ camera having support for Center Stage. Apple isn’t expected to make changes to the camera for the upcoming iPad. 
However, the company did change the Centre Stage camera with the arrival of the iPhone 17, and the new ‘square’ 18MP camera could be used on the front of the new iPad, but there are no reports indicating this will be the case. 
This front-facing camera has a larger, square sensor that supports automatic subject framing, orientation-agnostic capture, and advanced video features. On the iPad the 18MP camera could translate to improved video quality. However, current iPads already support smart framing during video calls so that aspect of the design may not be necessary. 


						

							


2027 iPad price: Will Apple keep the entry-level iPad affordable?
After launching at $449 in 2022, Apple cut the price of the entry-level iPad to $349 in May 2024, then doubled the starting storage from 64GB to 128GB with the 11th-generation model. However, in June 2026, Apple raised the price back to $449 due to supply-chain shortages. That makes the current A16 model considerably less attractive with a more capable, AI-ready replacement expected in early 2027. It’s also possible Apple could raise the price again when the new model arrives.

title: Apple Pushes Back Against Canada's Plan to Access User Data
content:
Apple is urging Canada to change a proposed law that it says could weaken the privacy and security protections built into its products.


The legislation, Bill C-22, is intended to help police and intelligence agencies obtain digital information during investigations. According to Bloomberg, Apple, Google, and Meta are lobbying for changes as Canadian senators review the bill.

At the center of the dispute is whether companies could be forced to change how their services work to help authorities access user data. The bill would allow the government to require companies to build tools for that purpose, with approval from Canada's Intelligence Commissioner.

It could also require certain providers to keep records about users' connections for up to six months. This metadata would exclude the contents of messages, browsing history, and social media activities.

added safeguards. For example, a company could only be required to unlock encrypted data if it supplied the encryption and already has the information needed to unlock it. The bill also says companies cannot be forced to introduce certain security weaknesses into their services.

Bloomberg that the bill would still undermine its ability to protect users' data. Apple previously warned that the legislation could let authorities demand backdoors.

title: Extensive new report claims Apple’s smart glasses will launch in June
content:
Macworld





A new report has leaked extensive details of Apple’s first set of smart glasses, which the company hopes to make the centerpiece of its 2027 product roster.
In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reveals that the project has been in development since the early 2020s and its hardware has been finished for some time; Apple, he claims, is waiting for the software to catch up before it makes the launch announcement. He expects this to happen at WWDC next year, in June 2027, with shipments to follow before the end of that year.
Delays, however, are still possible, because the software is currently “running behind.”
The importance of software to the project lies in the ability of Siri to trigger app-specific actions from voice commands alone. When wearing the glasses the user can issue a command to buy coffee (activating an action in the Starbucks app) or call a cab (in the Uber app) or book a restaurant reservation (in OpenTable). The product will rely on such interactions, and they still aren’t ready. But they’re close.
As Gurman explains, Siri AI has just gained a new AI-supported ability to agentically handle app-specific commands; this is part of the iOS 27.3 update, which is currently in beta and will likely roll out to the public in December. Now that developers have their hands on this upgrade they can build integrations for their own apps, which is nice for iPhone users, but will be absolutely vital for the success of Apple’s smart glasses.
There will be functions based on Apple’s own software, of course, such as Messages, Maps, and Visual Intelligence. But a product needs a deep third-party software ecosystem to become truly useful.
Software may be the key, but hardware will also be important to the device’s customer appeal. And here the glasses (which have frequently been referred to as Apple Glass, but are known internally as N50) may have more difficulty differentiating themselves from rival products. While the company has plans for “in-house-designed hardware, several style and color options, high-quality materials, additional sensors, and superior audio technology,” Gurman concedes that the overall presentation won’t differ very much from what Meta has offered for years or what Google is rolling out now.
“In terms of industrial design,” he writes, “internal prototypes are slightly thinner than Meta’s 2nd-generation Ray-Ban glasses. At least on some test units, the cameras are housed in oval-shaped openings that sit flush with the frame–rather than protruding from it. There’s also a light on the front that shows when the glasses are in use or charging.”
The audio at least should be premium-quality, and Apple may hope to set itself apart in this department, much as it attempted with the HomePod smart speakers. On the glasses the audio setup will support phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio. Gurman names the charging system as another highlight, based on a proprietary (oh dear) magnetic connector near the tip of one arm. It will actually be possible to wear the glasses and charge them at the same time, he reports.
What won’t be possible is to superimpose digital imagery over the user’s surroundings in the augmented-reality (AR) style. AR may be added in a future iteration but for the first generation, the glasses will deliver a more limited feature set. Gurman says this is why the product has internally been dubbed “AirPods for the face.” Many of the glasses’ capabilities will also be possible with a recent set of AirPods (particularly the upcoming camera-equipped models), albeit with weaker battery life and fewer sensors.
Apple is obviously close to unveiling its entry to yet another new market, following the iPhone Duo, HomeView, and touchscreen MacBook. Indeed the product’s existence was apparently revealed by a supplier last week. But the company wants to get everything in place for a smooth launch, so we’ll have to hang on just a little longer.

title: Apple's New HomeView Smart Home Hub Has Issues, Say Owners
content:

title: The new Apple TV 4K still has chip and RAM limitations
content:
Macworld





While it may have been overshadowed by the launch of the HomeView smart display, many Apple fans spent the weekend playing around with the other $300 smart home device that arrived last Friday: the new Apple TV 4K. 
The headline feature of the new device is the A19 chip and its 8GB of RAM. That’s a big upgrade over the previous generation’s A15 Bionic, which only had 4GB of RAM. This should make everything run faster, especially when playing games and other non-streaming apps.
Unfortunately, the performance gains might not be as big as you hope. For one, the A19 chip, which has a 6-core CPU with two performance cores and four efficiency cores in the iPhone 17 and 17e, is a new variant with just 5 CPU cores. According to pdfu on X, the A19 in the Apple TV 4K is a binned chip with one fewer efficiency core:
Two performance cores (4.260 GHz) 
Three efficiency​ cores (2.592 GHz) 
It does have the full 5-core GPU rather than the 4-core one used in the iPhone 17e. Apple used a similar configuration on the previous-generation Apple TV with a 5-core CPU that also had one high-efficiency core disabled.
While users probably won’t notice that missing core, they might notice another restriction on the new device. As reported by 9to5Mac, Apple is still limiting individual Apple TV apps from accessing more than 2GB of RAM due to Apple’s tvOS and API constraints. These restrictions have been in place for years, but with twice as much RAM available, we assumed Apple would lift or at least double this limitation to let developers create higher-end games and other experiences.
Alas, that’s not the case. So when you’re forking over $300 for a new Apple TV 4K, just know that you’re getting the same frustrating limitations as when it cost half as much.

The news answers recent uncertainty about the show's future. Cast member Olivia Cooke had suggested just days earlier that season eight could mark its conclusion.

The television series is catching up with the book series it is based on that began 16 years ago. Author Mick Herron has published nine main "Slough House" novels since the first one debuted in 2010, with gaps of between one and three years between installments. The latest, "Clown Town," arrived in 2025, three years after "Bad Actors."

Deadline that story details for the additional seasons would follow.

PRICES CHECKED 16 NOVEMBER, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy an Apple Watch, with retailers discounting everything from the affordable SE to the premium Ultra. Last year’s U.S. offers included $50 off the SE 3, up to $70 off the then-new Series 11, and $100 off the Ultra 3. Older models brought bigger savings, including $150 off the Series 10 and $200 off the Ultra 2. In the U.K., clearance offers were particularly attractive: the Series 10 was up to £130 off at Currys, while Argos cut £200 from the Ultra 2’s original price.
October Prime Day brought discounts on this year’s models, too. In the U.S., the 42mm Series 12 fell to $349, the 40mm SE 3 to $199, and the Ultra 4 to $774 – savings of $50, $50, and $25 respectively. U.K. highlights included the SE 3 at £199 and the previous-generation Series 11 at £259.
This Black Friday, we’d watch the Series 12 for discounts on our best Apple Watch for most people, the SE 3 for an affordable entry point, and the Ultra 4 for longer battery life and outdoor features. Remaining Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock could offer particularly good value if priced sufficiently below their replacements. Below, we explain which offers are worth taking and when to wait; for savings across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?


Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Series 12 is the Apple Watch we recommend for most people. It combines Apple’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate measurements, a Readiness score, and a tougher display with up to 24 hours of battery life.
A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.
U.S. Black Friday price: Amazon has already discounted the 42mm GPS Series 12 to $329, a savings of $70 and the best price we’ve ever seen. The 46mm version is also $70 off.
U.K. Black Friday price: We didn’t see Series 12 discounts during October Prime Day and so far this November there have been no price drops, but we are hopeful. We have only seen discounts on older models so far.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.
It’s more watch than most people need, but the current $699.99 offer is substantially below October Prime Day’s $774 price, making it worth considering if you want the latest Ultra. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the Ultra 4 down to $774, a $25 saving. This November we’ve already seen the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for $699.99 on Amazon: that’s $99 off. 
U.K. Black Friday price: The Ultra 4 remained at its full £749 price during October Prime Day, but we’ve already seen it drop by £20 to £729 at Amazon. 


						

							


Apple Watch SE 3 – Our best budget choice

				
					

				
			
Apple / Amazon




The SE 3 is the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience. It includes an always-on display, temperature sensing, fast charging, and the S10 chip, but lacks ECG, blood oxygen monitoring, and the newer Health Sensing System.
It remains part of Apple’s current lineup despite launching in 2025. A strong Black Friday offer could make it an excellent affordable purchase, although its previous discounts mean there’s little reason to settle for a token reduction.
U.S. Black Friday price: Both last Black Friday and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to $199 and the 44mm version to $229 – $50 below their regular prices. So far, the U.S. price drop is just $9 at Amazon, so we’d hold out for bigger savings.
U.K. Black Friday price: Black Friday 2025 and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to £199 and the 44mm version to £229, saving £20. So far we haven’t seen any price drops for Black Friday 2026.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 3 – Best clearance option for outdoor enthusiasts

				
					

				
			
Apple




The Ultra 3 is worth considering if you want a rugged Apple Watch without paying for the latest model. It offers satellite communication, dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and up to 42 hours of battery life.
You give up the Ultra 4’s longer battery life and newer Health Sensing System. Compare their actual selling prices: the Ultra 3 needs to be sufficiently cheaper to justify choosing the older generation.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 fell to $699, a $100 saving. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models, so it didn’t identify a comparable new-stock offer. So far this November we’ve seen the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $649, but that’s out of stock now.

Apple Watch Series 11 – Best clearance option for everyday use

				
					

				
			
Apple Watch Series 11




The Series 11 could be a better-value everyday watch than the Series 12 if the price gap is large enough. It has the same quoted 24-hour battery life, although it misses the newer Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features.
For buyers who don’t need those additions, a substantial clearance discount could be more useful than a small saving on the latest model.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the 42mm GPS Series 11 reached $339, while the 46mm version was $359 – savings of $60 and $70, respectively. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models in the U.S. and so far that’s all we are seeing this November.

Last Black Friday’s bigger clearance offers were on the preceding Series 10, which was available for £279 in 42mm and £299 in 46mm. In November 2026 you can get a Series 11 for £299, £120 less than the equivalent Series 12.

Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.
October Prime Day prices provide useful benchmarks. In the U.S., the Series 12 fell to $349 for the 42mm GPS model and $399 for the 46mm version, while the Ultra 4 reached $774. The SE 3 was $199 in 40mm and $229 in 44mm. Those SE prices also appeared last Black Friday, so we’d look for offers matching or beating them. In the U.K., October highlights included the 40mm SE 3 at £199 and the older 42mm Series 11 at £259.
The Series 12 and Ultra 4 only arrived in September, so finding a better price is the main reason to wait. If you don’t need a watch immediately, those previous offers give you a useful starting point for deciding whether to buy now or hold out.
Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.


						

							


Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.
Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.
The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.


						

							


Apple Watch deals to avoid 

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.
Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Our GPS versus cellular Apple Watch guide explains the trade-offs.
Check the rest of the configuration, too. A premium case material or expensive band can make a heavily discounted watch cost more than a simpler version that meets your needs. Judge offers against previous selling prices as well as the advertised reduction: a large saving from the original launch price doesn’t necessarily mean exceptional value. Check any spending requirements, contracts, trade-ins, or rebates attached to offers advertising a “free” Apple Watch.
Finally, check whether you’re buying a new, refurbished, or used watch, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For a used or refurbished model, check the stated battery condition and confirm that it has been removed from the previous owner’s account and Activation Lock. Make sure the watch is compatible with your iPhone before ordering.


						

							


How we choose Apple Watch deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on Apple Watch reviews and everyday wear. We consider comfort, performance, battery life, charging, health and fitness features, and value – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our Series 12 review assessed battery life and charging performance alongside its newer health features. We also draw on everyday experience: our cellular Apple Watch testing examines whether staying connected without an iPhone justified the extra hardware and subscription costs.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. We check the generation, case size, material, connectivity, and included band so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside discounted replacements.
Our Best Apple Watch guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the right choice: your budget, wrist size, activities, and the features you need all matter.
For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our roundups of the best Mac deals, iPad deals, and AirPods deals.

PRICES CHECKED NOVEMBER 16 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy AirPods, with retailers competing to offer discounts across Apple’s earbuds and over-ear headphones. Previous sales have brought substantial savings on established models, clearance bargains on older generations, and even discounts on newly released AirPods. But the biggest percentage saving doesn’t necessarily mean the best buy: an older pair needs to be sufficiently cheaper than its replacement to justify missing out on newer features.
Last Black Friday, standard AirPods 4 briefly dropped to $69 in the U.S., while the noise-canceling version fell to $99 – an $80 saving. Even the then-new AirPods Pro 3 received a discount of around $30, while older AirPods Pro 2 reached approximately $139 before selling out. AirPods Max were available for around $400, roughly $150 below their regular price. U.K. savings were more modest, with AirPods 4 at £99 and AirPods Pro 2 at £169, although stock frequently ran out.
This year, we’d watch AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 for meaningful discounts, while remaining AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 stock could bring some of the biggest clearance savings. The recently released AirPods 5 may see smaller reductions, making it especially important to compare their price with discounted Pro models. Below, we explain which AirPods to choose and how the offers compare with previous discounts. For savings on Macs, iPads, Apple Watch and more, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which AirPods should you buy this Black Friday?


AirPods Pro 3 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Pro 3 are especially worth considering if you want strong noise cancellation, a secure in-ear fit, or Apple’s hearing-health features. Their foam-infused ear tips help improve the fit, while an in-ear heart-rate sensor adds another reason to choose them over standard AirPods. Battery life is rated at up to eight hours with noise cancellation enabled.
For most buyers looking for noise-isolating earbuds, these would be our first choice. Older AirPods Pro 2 are worth considering only when the clearance savings are substantial.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has already slashed almost $70 off the AirPods Pro 3, but we expect the price to go lower. Hopefully, by Black Friday, they will hit their all-time low of $169.
U.K. Black Friday price: In the U.K. earlier in November there was £30 off the AirPods Pro 3, but they are now £200, which is a slightly less impressive £19 off.


						

							


AirPods 5 – Best for buyers who prefer earbuds without silicone tips

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods 5 offer a lower-cost entry point and an open-ear design for people who don’t like silicone-tipped earbuds. They include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, alongside Transparency mode and Adaptive Audio.
Check which charging case you’re buying. The Wireless Charging Case package adds wireless charging, longer battery life, a Find My speaker, and volume adjustment by swiping the stems. It’s our preferred package when the price difference is small.
U.S. Black Friday price: We’ve not seen a discount yet on the AirPods 5.
U.K. Black Friday price:  No savings yet on the AirPods 5.


						

							


AirPods Max 2 – Best for over-ear listening

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Max 2 are the option to consider if you specifically want over-ear headphones. The March 2026 update introduced Apple’s H2 chip and improved noise cancellation, while retaining the premium design and a choice of colors.
We find them difficult to recommend at full price, so the size of the discount matters. Compare any offer with previous sale prices rather than judging it solely against Apple’s asking price.

U.K. Black Friday price:  The AirPods Max 2 are £449 at Amazon – that’s £50 off. You can get the same deal at AO and Boots.

Apple

Check the exact generation, charging case, condition, and seller before buying. For more help choosing, read our AirPods buying guide.

Beats




If AirPods aren’t in your budget, Apple also sells a line of Beats headphones and earbuds that offer many of the same features for a lower price, including the popular over-ear Solo 4 and PowerBeats Pro 2. David Price / Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need AirPods immediately. But the sales now stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer is close to a model’s previous low, it can be worth taking: last year’s best deals frequently sold out, and popular offers could go quickly again.
Previous sale prices provide useful benchmarks. We’ve seen AirPods Pro 3 reach $169, while AirPods Max 2 fell to $399 during June Prime Day. An offer above those prices may still be worth considering, but a reduction from Apple’s regular price doesn’t automatically make it an exceptional deal.
For AirPods 5, waiting for a discount makes sense if you aren’t in a hurry: they didn’t receive a significant reduction during October Prime Day. With AirPods Max 2, we’d hold out for a substantial saving rather than pay full price.
Compare retailers, too. Amazon isn’t always cheapest: Walmart and Best Buy also compete on AirPods pricing, while Argos offered competitive U.K. deals last year. Our guide to the best time to buy AirPods has more advice on purchase timing.


						

							


Should you buy an old pair of AirPods? 
Older-generation AirPods can be a good buy at the right clearance price. Compare their actual selling price with the discounted price of their replacement, rather than focusing on the percentage saving from an old launch price. A substantial discount can make an older pair worthwhile; a small difference may leave you sacrificing useful features for little saving.
AirPods 4 are harder to recommend now that AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, starting at the same $129 price previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC. Check which AirPods 4 version you’re buying—there were models with and without noise cancellation—and look for a substantial saving over AirPods 5.
AirPods Pro 2 remain worth considering if they’re significantly cheaper than Pro 3. However, the newer model improves fit, noise cancellation, and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing. Compare their sale prices carefully: a strong Pro 3 discount could make the older pair’s clearance offer less attractive.
The original AirPods Max also need a substantial discount to justify choosing them over Max 2. The newer headphones add the H2 chip, improved noise cancellation, and features including Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. Check the generation rather than relying on the charging port alone: the original AirPods Max were also sold in a USB-C version.
Buying older stock new is different from buying used or refurbished AirPods. For those pairs, check the stated condition, charging case, warranty, and returns policy, and buy from a reputable seller. Be cautious about battery condition and unusually low marketplace prices, since convincing counterfeits can resemble genuine AirPods. Our guide explains how to spot fake AirPods.
For more advice, see our AirPods buying guide and guide to the best time to buy AirPods.


						

							


AirPods deals to avoid

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Check exactly what an offer includes before comparing prices. Different charging-case packages can affect features and value, so make sure you’re comparing equivalent versions. Also check any spending requirements, contracts, or rebates attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods.
Judge the price against previous selling prices as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.
Check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair. For used or refurbished AirPods, look for clear information about condition, warranty, and returns coverage. Battery condition deserves particular caution: a low purchase price may be less attractive if listening time has deteriorated.
Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Unusually low prices from unfamiliar sellers warrant caution, since counterfeit AirPods can look convincing. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.


						

							


How we choose AirPods deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. Our Best AirPods guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the best choice for everyone: fit, listening habits, and the features you need all matter.

This Black Friday, we’d watch the M4 iPad Air for a balance of performance and price, the A16 iPad for a worthwhile budget deal, and the M5 iPad Pro for buyers who need its premium capabilities. The new A20 Pro iPad mini, with its OLED display, also changes the calculation: we’d expect smaller initial discounts on the new arrival, while remaining A17 Pro stock could offer clearance bargains. Below, we explain which deals are worth taking, checking the generation, storage, and connectivity rather than simply choosing the biggest advertised saving. For offers across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which iPad should you buy this Black Friday?


M4 iPad Air – Our best all-round choice

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Air offers a strong balance of performance, screen size, and price without the premium cost of the Pro. The 11-inch model suits buyers who prioritize portability, while the 13-inch version gives you more room for multitasking and creative work.
A good Black Friday discount could make either size an attractive purchase. Compare storage capacities carefully, though: a larger advertised saving on a high-capacity model isn’t necessarily better value if you don’t need the extra space.

iPad Pro – Best for demanding creative work

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Pro is the option for buyers who need Apple’s highest-end tablet performance and premium display. It comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, but its capabilities – and price – will exceed what many people need for browsing, streaming, and everyday apps.
We’d look for a substantial saving rather than buy simply because it’s the most powerful iPad. Compare discounted M4 Pro stock, too: an older Pro could offer better value if its price is sufficiently below the equivalent M5 configuration.

Apple
