Should you buy an iPad now or wait for a better deal?

				
					

				
			
There’s an iPad for everyone.

Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an iPad immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if the price is competitive. Compare the exact generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity rather than waiting for Black Friday simply because a larger discount might appear.
Previous selling prices are particularly important this year because Apple raised iPad prices in June. During October Prime Day, the 128GB A16 iPad was $399, while the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB was $649. Both were discounted against Apple’s increased prices, but cost more than their regular prices before June. A saving from today’s asking price doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting an exceptional bargain.
For the M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro, we’d focus on finding a good price: our guide to the best time to buy an iPad doesn’t expect replacements until 2027. We’d be more cautious about the A16 iPad, which lacks Apple Intelligence and is expected to be replaced. Unless you find a substantial saving, waiting could get you a more capable entry-level model.
The new A20 Pro iPad mini presents a different decision. It has only just arrived, so we’d expect smaller initial discounts rather than immediate clearance-level savings. If you want its OLED display and newer processor, a modest reduction may still be worthwhile. If price matters more, compare remaining A17 Pro stock – but make sure the saving justifies choosing the older hardware.


						

							


Should you buy an older iPad? 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older iPad can be a good buy if its price reflects its age and the features you give up. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of its replacement, matching screen size, storage, and connectivity where possible. A large saving from an old launch price doesn’t necessarily make it better value.
The M3 iPad Air and M4 iPad Pro are worth considering at substantial clearance discounts. Both remain capable options, and you may get more benefit from a lower price or additional storage than from the latest processor. However, if the newer equivalent costs only slightly more, the saving may not justify choosing the older generation.
The A17 Pro iPad mini also deserves consideration now that the A20 Pro model has arrived. It supports Apple Intelligence and remains a capable compact tablet, but you miss the newer model’s OLED display, faster processor, and thinner, lighter design. We’d want a meaningful saving rather than a small reduction from its former asking price.
Be more cautious with much older models. Check whether they support the current version of iPadOS and the apps and features you need. Compatibility today doesn’t guarantee how many future software upgrades they’ll receive. Apple Intelligence support also varies: don’t assume every older Air, Pro, or mini includes it.
If you already own an Apple Pencil or keyboard, check compatibility before changing generations. Keeping compatible accessories could make an older iPad better value, while replacing them could erase part of your saving. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges.


						

							


iPad deals to avoid
Check the exact configuration before comparing offers. Retailer listings can emphasize iPad, Air, or Pro without making the generation obvious. Confirm the chip, screen size, storage capacity, and whether you’re buying Wi-Fi or Wi-Fi + Cellular. A cheaper listing may be a different model rather than a better deal.
Don’t let a large advertised discount tempt you into paying for storage or connectivity you won’t use. A heavily reduced high-capacity or cellular iPad can still cost more than a simpler configuration that meets your needs. Compare the final purchase prices, rather than assuming the biggest saving represents the best value.
Check whether the price includes nano-texture glass, too. This optional finish reduces glare and makes fingerprints and oily smudges less noticeable, which can be useful if reflections make your iPad difficult to see in bright rooms or outdoors. It avoids much of the washed-out appearance associated with ordinary matte finishes, but contrast can drop at some viewing angles and the surface may be more scratch-sensitive. Availability depends on the model and storage configuration, so you could end up paying for both the finish and additional storage. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may be better value. Read our guide to nano-texture glass and whether you need it.
Our iPad buying guide considers cellular a luxury for most buyers. If you mainly use your iPad somewhere with Wi-Fi, you may get little benefit from the extra hardware. For occasional use elsewhere, sharing your iPhone’s connection through Personal Hotspot can be a more economical option.
Cellular makes more sense if you regularly need an independent connection while commuting or traveling; it also adds built-in GPS for accurate location tracking. Factor in any data-plan charges and compare the total cost of a contract with buying outright. A cellular model can still be worthwhile if its sale price matches or beats the equivalent Wi-Fi version—you don’t have to activate a data plan simply because the hardware is included.
Judge savings against previous selling prices as well as Apple’s current price. Following June’s price increases, a discounted iPad may still cost more than it did earlier in the year. Also distinguish a cash discount from a gift-card offer: a gift card doesn’t reduce the amount you pay for the iPad and is useful only if you’ll spend it.
Check what any bundle includes. A keyboard, case, or stylus doesn’t automatically make an offer better value, particularly if the accessories aren’t the versions you want. Read the conditions attached to “free” iPads, trade-in promotions, contracts, and rebates before comparing their total cost with buying outright.
Finally, check whether the iPad is new, refurbished, or used, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For used or refurbished models, look for information about battery condition and confirm that Activation Lock has been removed. Be cautious about devices that remain tied to a previous owner or an organization’s management system.


						

							


How we choose iPad deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on iPad reviews and everyday use. We consider performance, display quality, portability, battery life, and accessory support alongside price to explain which iPads suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess whether paying more brings practical benefits. A faster processor or premium display may matter for demanding creative work, while a less expensive iPad can be perfectly capable of browsing, streaming, and schoolwork. We also consider the cost of keyboards, Apple Pencils, and other accessories when judging an iPad’s value.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than relying solely on savings against today’s recommended price.
Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside newer alternatives. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges, while our purchase-timing guide helps you decide whether to buy now or wait.
For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our roundups of the best Mac deals, AirPods deals, and Apple Watch deals.

title: New Apple health study wants to find out how much you trust AI
content:
Apple has launched a year-long research project into how people trust AI and use it for health advice, since users keep turning to chatbots despite repeated examples of dangerous results.


Apple's new health study app - image credit: Apple
It's hardly a secret that AI gets things wrong, but still there are cases such as ChatGPT dissuading a pastor from getting his cardiac issue attended to. Giving your health data to ChatGPT is an all-round bad idea, yet it hasn't been blocked from being connected to Apple Health.
Now Apple has launched what it's calling the Apple Health AI Usage Study to examine how users work with health AI chatbots. It's intended to help with making AI health more responsible.

title: We finally found something Apple’s tech rivals are better at: Scandals
content:
Macworld





Wow! What a week that was for fans of the classic tech-industry scandal: In the space of six days, Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia each launched a high-profile new PR controversy to the world’s media. Much as I enjoyed the fallout, however, it saddens me as a long-term Cupertino watcher to report that Apple has clearly fallen behind in this vital market.
Indeed, we must now ask ourselves if Apple is any longer capable of competing with its rivals in the development and manufacture of top-quality bungles and blunders.
The week began with a confession by Jensen Huang, the centibillionaire Nvidia founder and walking midlife crisis, who admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Later in the week, The New York Times claimed Huang had also had an affair with a married coworker who reported to him; a day later Reuters reported that he also had an affair with a second Nvidia employee.
It’s difficult to see where Huang found the time to run the company, but following a speedy resignation that is no longer his affair, as it were. (It’s believed, incidentally, that Apple hardware boss Johny Srouji is on the short list of candidates for the job. Lucky him.)
The week ended with a very different sort of tech debacle, as server problems at Microsoft led to major issues hitting pretty much the whole internet. Anyone relying on Outlook email or other Microsoft 365 services faced lengthy outages, as did users of apps and services which in turn depend on Microsoft’s servers, such as OpenAI and Anthropic’s AI assistants. Businesses, schools and public services were affected for large sections of Thursday and Friday; worse still, Macworld reporters were unable to have virtual meetings. It was a relatively big inconvenience for a huge number of people for an unacceptably long time.
At the time of writing, it remains unclear, beyond the vague explanation that a server process became overwhelmed, what exactly went wrong. And as ever, social media coverage expanded to fill the vacuum. Many blamed the company’s extensive job cuts this year, and its supposed reliance on AI and vibe-coding. Macworld has not seen any conclusive evidence that these factors were relevant, but in the scandal business, feelings don’t care about your facts, or lack of them. And whatever the reason, the reputational damage will be brutal, as the internet ponders whether it can ever again rely on Microsoft to underpin its most vital processes.
In between Nvidia’s humiliation and Microsoft’s vilification, Apple stepped in with a PR drama which, by comparison, seems almost quaint: Some retail employees allegedly signed up customers to recurring subscription services without informed consent. It’s a serious matter, and one which reflects poorly on Apple’s training and incentivisation of its staff. But the headlines and social media catastrophising simply couldn’t compare with the week’s bigger and more lurid stories.
It’s not like Apple doesn’t release its fair share of screw-ups and blunders, they just don’t cut through to the mainstream the way they used to. We had iPhone Duo screen breakages earlier this fall, for example, but the outrage was limited because not many people had enough money to buy one. (By comparison, the Microsoft outage has achieved such widespread awareness that my mother sent me a message about it while I was writing this article.) And ultimately it was just a relatively small hardware problem, much like Antennagate and Bendgate. There was no novelty, no human interest. Nobody was caught sleeping with a spy and two coworkers. Allegedly.
It’s a truism in media that Apple gets more coverage than it deserves. For better and for worse, its corporate snafus as much as its successful product launches are automatically considered newsworthy. Think back to the stories in 2020 about forced labor in China, which all prominently mentioned Apple despite it being only one of 83 “well-known global brands” to be involved. Or the lack of interest when Samsung dropped the headphone port from its phones in 2019, even though everyone, including Samsung, lost their mind when Apple did the same thing three years earlier.
To a great extent, that remains true. You’ll still read coverage of the latest iPhone launch on mainstream news sites, which would never write about Nvidia’s chips or Microsoft’s cloud services. As a maker of products, Apple remains the biggest show in town. But the news cycle is hungry for something juicier than products.
The tech industry has changed a great deal since Apple was founded in 1976: It’s a lot more glamorous, considerably sillier, and above all peopled with far more toxic personalities. Tech CEOs in the 70s were boring suits, not dangerous weirdoes. They were less prone to dabble in politics; few, if any, of them got quoted in the papers complaining about the energy cost of humans. But times have changed: thanks to the influence of social media and the attention economy, today’s public demands a higher standard of PR disaster. And it seems that Apple, with its cautious media operations and succession of safe-pair-of-hands CEOs, has got left behind.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Welcome to our weekly Apple Breakfast column, which includes all the Apple news you missed last week in a handy bite-sized roundup. We call it Apple Breakfast because we think it goes great with a Monday morning cup of coffee or tea, but it’s cool if you want to give it a read during lunch or dinner hours too.
Trending: Top stories
The Macalope has never been happier that Apple is bad at AI.
The iPhone 18 Pro has one job: Keep selling Duos.
HomeView is Apple’s first post-iPhone device. But it has one big problem: the iPad.
Wow! The new MacBook Pro has a brilliant cooling system.
Subscription scandal reveals the dark side of Apple’s pivot to services.
Apple TV 4K needs a downgrade, argues Felipe Esposito. Yes, a downgrade.
Podcast of the week
In the latest episode of the Macworld Podcast, we talk about our experience with Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED Display. Why we like the laptop, what macOS Touch is all about, and our recommendation.






You can catch every episode of the Macworld Podcast on YouTube, Spotify, Soundcloud, the Podcasts app, or our own site.
Reviews corner
16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display: Simply irresistible.
SanDisk Extreme Pro SSD: Fast, rugged, and expensive.
Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger: An Apple charging station with room for iPad.
The rumor mill
Agentic Siri is coming, and that’s just the beginning, says Jason Cross.
Apple’s rumored smart glasses were just confirmed by a supplier. Whoops!
Apple is reportedly set to eliminate the Action button and combine its functions with the Camera button.
Video of the week
“An extremely appropriately named product.” Check out Jason Cross’s verdict on the iPhone Duo. For more videos, follow us on TikTok and Instagram.






Software updates, bugs, and problems
Apple suddenly shutters its Support Community forums for no clear reason.
Nvidia’s CEO scandal could have major repercussions at Apple Park.
If your old printer stopped working with macOS 27, there’s an easy fix.
macOS 27.3 increases security with changes to Full Disk Access 18.7.12.
And with that, we’re done for this week’s Apple Breakfast. If you’d like to get regular roundups, sign up for our newsletters, including our new email from The Macalope–an irreverent, humorous take on the latest news and rumors from a half-man, half-mythical Mac beast. You can also follow us on Facebook, Threads, Bluesky, or X for discussion of breaking Apple news stories. See you next Monday, and stay Appley.

PRICES CHECKED NOVEMBER 16, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is one of the best opportunities to save on a Mac, with retailers competing to discount MacBooks and desktop models – including recently released machines. Last year, U.S. shoppers could get a 13-inch M4 MacBook Air for $749, saving $250, while the then-new 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro fell to $1,349, also $250 off. Selected M4 Max MacBook Pro configurations received $500 discounts. U.K. highlights included £150 off the entry-level M4 MacBook Air and savings of around £350 on selected MacBook Pro models.
This year’s deals need a different perspective because Apple raised Mac prices in June. The MacBook Air went up by $200/£200, while some MacBook Pro configurations increased by as much as $500/£500. October Prime Day helped offset those increases: the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with 512GB storage fell to $1,099, saving $200, while selected high-end MacBook Pros received discounts of up to $600. Desktop offers included around $120 off the entry-level M6 Mac mini and $200 off the M5 Max Mac Studio.
Those increases mean we may not see a return to earlier record-low prices this Black Friday, even when retailers offer substantial discounts. However, November’s sales could still bring some of the best prices available under Apple’s higher pricing, making this a worthwhile time to buy if you need a new Mac. We’re comparing current offers with previous selling prices and equivalent configurations – not simply the biggest advertised saving – to help you identify genuine value. Below, you’ll find our picks across MacBooks and desktop Macs; for discounts on Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which Mac or MacBook should you buy this Black Friday?


MacBook Air – Our best overall choice 

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most buyers. Both sizes offer a lightweight, silent laptop for everyday work, studying, and occasional creative projects. Choose the 13-inch for portability or the 15-inch for more workspace without MacBook Pro pricing.
We’d prioritize a competitive price on the memory and storage you need. For regular lengthy exports or other sustained demanding tasks, consider a MacBook Pro with active cooling instead.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the 13-inch M5 Air with 16GB memory and 512GB storage to $1,099, and the equivalent 15-inch to $1,299. Last Black Friday, the older M4 models with 256GB reached $749 and $949 respectively. We are already seeing up to $250 off the 1TB models, and $200 off the 512GB options, bringing the price back to the original MSRP before Apple increased prices.  
U.K. Black Friday price: October offers included approximately £1,199 for the 13-inch M5 Air and £1,349 for the 15-inch, both with 512GB storage. Last Black Friday’s M4 models with 256GB reached £849 and £1,025. Match storage capacities when comparing generations. So far in November 2026 we are seeing the same £200 off the 13-inch MacBook Air and £200 off the 15-inch model which are better than what we saw for Prime Day this October. 


						

							


MacBook Neo – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




The MacBook Neo suits browsing, schoolwork, streaming, and office apps. Its lower starting price makes it appealing, but its fixed 8GB of memory leaves less room for demanding workloads.
Check which configuration is discounted: only the 512GB version includes Touch ID. Both lack a backlit keyboard, MagSafe, and Thunderbolt. Compare clearance MacBook Air stock before deciding how much those compromises save you.
U.S. Black Friday price: October’s $689 price for the 256GB Neo was only a small reduction from its $699 asking price and the current $13 saving is equally small.
U.K. Black Friday price: We saw a Prime Day low of £549, but that was before Apple increased prices. Now the low is £649, £50 off for the 256GB model. We are also seeing £79 off the 512GB MacBook Neo. 


						

							


MacBook Pro M6 – Best step up from the Air

				
					

				
			
Macbook Pro M6 Aufmacher

Halyna Kubiv




The standard M6 MacBook Pro is worth considering if you want a better built-in display, more connections, and cooling for sustained workloads without paying for a Pro or Max chip. It comes in a 14-inch size, with a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot.
It starts with 16GB memory and 1TB storage, so account for those specifications when comparing prices with an Air or older Pro. Despite the newer generation number, the standard M6 isn’t automatically the better choice for demanding work than an M5 Pro or M5 Max.
U.S. Black Friday price: The M6 model wasn’t available during October Prime Day. Its M5 predecessor with 16GB memory and 1TB storage reached $1,839. We aren’t seeing discounts on the M6 yet, but you can get the 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro for $200 less than the new model. 
U.K. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the older 14-inch M5 with 16GB memory and 1TB storage reached approximately £1,619. We are already seeing £169 off the 14-inch, M6 with 1TB, 16GB, also note that it is only £31.97 more than the M5 (£1,830.97 versus £1,799), so we wouldn’t recommend the older model. 


						

							


MacBook Pro M5 Pro – Best for demanding professional work

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The non-touchscreen M5 Pro MacBook Pro is a strong choice for development, photography, video editing, and heavier multitasking. Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, it offers professional performance without the Max chip’s higher price.
Compare it with the touchscreen version using the same memory and storage. Both offer M5 Pro configurations, so a discounted non-touch model could be particularly good value if its existing XDR display meets your needs.
U.S. Black Friday price: October prices included $2,339 for the 14-inch M5 Pro with 24GB memory and 1TB storage, and $2,749 for the equivalent 16-inch. So far this Black Friday month we are seeing $250 off the 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 1TB).
U.K. Black Friday price: The equivalent configurations reached approximately £2,250 and £2,700. Last Black Friday, selected previous-generation M4 Pro models received discounts of around £350. So far this Black Friday there is a £349 saving on the 16-inch M5 Pro model. Note that the 14-inch M5 Pro, 2TB/24GB model is only £24.03 more than the 1TB/24GB version.


						

							


MacBook Pro M5 Max – Best for demanding graphics and video

				
					

				
			
Stephan Wiesend




Consider the non-touchscreen M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work benefits from additional graphics power or more memory than an M5 Pro supports. Complex 3D projects and demanding video production make a stronger case for it than everyday productivity.
We’d choose the configuration around the work you do. A larger advertised discount on a Max doesn’t necessarily make it better value than a less expensive Pro that meets your needs. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the options.
U.S. Black Friday price:  October offers included $3,499 for a 14-inch M5 Max with 2TB storage and $3,899 for a 16-inch with 36GB memory and 2TB storage. Last Black Friday, selected M4 Max configurations were $500 off and this Black Friday month we are already seeing $500 off the M5 Max models. 
U.K. Black Friday price:  October coverage included a 14-inch M5 Max with 2TB storage at £3,799, saving £300. This time there is £100 off the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5 Max.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro – Best for its OLED display

				
					

				
			


Roman Loyola/Foundry




The touchscreen MacBook Pro is most compelling for its OLED display and thinner, lighter design. Improved blacks and reduced blooming could matter more to your everyday experience than touch controls, particularly if you spend most of your working day using the built-in screen.
Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes with M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, these models offer comparable processing performance to their non-touch equivalents. Compare matching configurations: the regular premium is $400/£400, so consider how much you’ll benefit from the display before paying extra.
U.S. Black Friday price:  These models arrived in November, so there are no equivalent October Prime Day or Black Friday 2025 prices. Compare any offer with the matching non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model. It’s early days so we don’t expect to see big savings here this Black Friday. 
U.K. Black Friday price: We don’t expect to see significant price drops since these Macs launched so recently. 


						

							


Mac mini M6 – Our best-value desktop choice

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The M6 Mac mini suits buyers who already own a display, keyboard, and mouse. It offers a compact desktop for everyday work and lighter creative projects. Check storage carefully: the entry-level model has a restrictive 256GB SSD.
U.S. Black Friday price: October’s entry-level M6 mini reached approximately $780. Last Black Friday, the older M4 equivalent was $479. So far this November we’ve seen $150 off the 512GB model.
U.K. Black Friday price: October’s M6 model reached approximately £824, compared with £499 for the M4 last Black Friday. There’s £100 off the 250GB Mac mini in the U.K.


						

							


Mac mini M5 Pro – Best compact desktop for professional work

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




The M5 Pro mini offers more processing power and memory capacity for demanding work without moving to a Studio. Compare upgraded configurations carefully: if the total approaches Mac Studio pricing, check which machine better suits your workload.
U.S. Black Friday price: The 24GB/512GB M5 Pro mini reached approximately $1,550 in October. Last Black Friday’s M4 Pro equivalent was $1,249. So far this November we’ve seen $150 off the 512GB model.
U.K. Black Friday price: October’s M5 Pro configuration reached approximately £1,647. The previous-generation M4 Pro with 24GB/512GB was £1,269 last Black Friday. There is £150 off the 512GB Mac mini M5 Pro in the U.K. 


						

							


iMac – Best complete desktop setup

				
					

				
			

Foundry




The iMac combines a 24-inch 4.5K display with the computer and matching accessories. Compare the two-port and four-port versions carefully: the latter adds processing power, connections, and a Touch ID keyboard. Factor those differences into the final price.
U.S. Black Friday price: The M6 wasn’t available during October Prime Day. The entry-level M4 predecessor reached approximately $1,360 in October and $1,149 last Black Friday. We’ve not seen any savings yet. 
U.K. Black Friday price: October’s four-port M4 with 256GB storage was £1,620. Last Black Friday, comparable four-port M4 stock reached £1,349. These are predecessor prices rather than M6 targets. The new iMac models aren’t discounted at the moment. 


						

							


Mac Studio – Best for demanding desktop workflows

Should you buy a Mac or MacBook now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need a Mac immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if it matches or approaches a previous low for the same configuration. Waiting can be a gamble if you’re buying clearance stock with a particular screen size, memory capacity, or finish.
The M5 MacBook Air remains an appealing purchase at a good discount, with a replacement not expected until 2027. The recently updated Mac mini and Mac Studio are also worth considering if they meet your needs. The main reason to wait is a better price rather than an imminent replacement.
MacBook Pro buyers no longer need to wait for the rumored October launches: the standard M6 and OLED touchscreen models are now available. However, their recent arrival may limit initial discounts. Non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer better value, particularly if you don’t need the touchscreen version’s improved display and lighter design. If your existing M4 or M5 MacBook Pro still meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade simply because a newer option exists.
The M6 iMac has only just arrived, replacing the aging M4 version. Compare a modest saving on the latest model with a substantial clearance discount on its predecessor, rather than assuming the older machine is automatically the better deal.
Previous prices need context this year. Following June’s increases, a discount from Apple’s current asking price may still leave you paying more than before the increases. Compare retailers as well: Amazon competes with Best Buy, Walmart, and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys and John Lewis in the U.K. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the current choices.


						

							


Which Mac specifications are worth paying for?
The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Use Black Friday to get a configuration that will serve you for longer within your budget, but don’t pay for performance or features you won’t use.
Check the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. A standard M6 and an M5 Pro or M5 Max serve different needs: the newer generation number alone doesn’t tell you which is better for your work. For MacBook Pro listings, distinguish the OLED touchscreen version from non-touch models.
Avoid saving a small amount by buying too little memory or storage. Most current Macs start with 16GB of unified memory, but the MacBook Neo has a fixed 8GB, and some desktop configurations include only a 256GB SSD. Unified memory cannot be upgraded later. An external SSD can add storage, but it cannot compensate for insufficient RAM.
Once the processor meets your needs, additional memory may be more useful than a faster chip. Compare a discounted Air with the Neo, too: the M5 Air starts with twice the memory and storage of the entry-level Neo. Our Mac buying guide explains which specifications suit different workloads.
Check whether the configuration includes nano-texture glass. This optional finish reduces glare and reflections, which can help in bright rooms or near windows, but increases the price. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may offer better value.


						

							


Should you buy an older Mac or MacBook?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older Mac can be excellent value if its price reflects its age and configuration. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of the newer equivalent, rather than focusing on a large percentage saving from its original launch price.
Previous-generation Apple silicon models are the most promising starting point. A discounted M4 MacBook Air or standard M5 MacBook Pro may meet your needs comfortably. Older Pro and Max configurations can also be worth considering if they provide the memory, graphics performance, and connections your work requires for substantially less money.
Check what the saving buys—and what you give up. An older Mac with more memory or storage could be more useful than a newer entry-level configuration. Conversely, a cheaper older Air with 256GB storage isn’t directly comparable with an M5 Air that starts with 512GB. The non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros also remain current options, despite the arrival of the standard M6 and touchscreen models.
Be much more cautious with Intel Macs. Their software support is winding down, and a low purchase price may leave you with a machine that has a limited useful life for current apps and macOS features. Check compatibility with the software you need before buying any older model.
For used or refurbished Macs, check battery condition on laptops, warranty coverage, and the returns policy. Confirm that Activation Lock has been removed and that the Mac isn’t still enrolled in an organization’s management system.

Should I buy a Mac Studio?


						

							


Mac or MacBook deals to avoid
Treat large advertised discounts carefully. Following June’s price increases, “$400 off” may simply bring a Mac closer to what it cost before the increase. Compare previous selling prices for the same configuration, rather than judging the offer solely against today’s recommended price.
Check whether the price includes AppleCare+ or another protection plan. Some Amazon listings bundle coverage with the Mac. If you don’t want it, a listing without coverage could be cheaper; if you do, compare the bundle with buying the Mac and coverage separately.
Check for a bundled power adapter, too. Some Mac laptops are sold without one in the U.K. and EU. A charger bundle may be useful if you need an adapter, but could mean paying extra unnecessarily if you already own a suitable one.
Compare the complete setup cost. A Mac mini or Studio requires a display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad, while adapters and docks can add to the cost of any Mac.
Finally, distinguish cash discounts from gift cards, trade-ins, financing, and membership-only offers. Read the conditions, check the seller, and confirm whether the Mac is new, refurbished, or used, along with its warranty and returns policy.


						

							


How we choose Mac and MacBook deals
Macworld has covered the Mac since its launch in 1984, and our recommendations draw on decades of experience and hands-on reviews. We consider performance, display quality, battery life, portability, connectivity, and everyday use alongside price to explain which Macs suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess which upgrades are worth paying for. We look at whether additional processing power benefits demanding workloads, when more memory is useful, and whether a premium display justifies the extra cost. A MacBook Air may offer better value for everyday work, while a Pro, Max, or Ultra configuration needs to earn its higher price through the work it enables.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than judging a deal solely against today’s recommended retail price. A large advertised discount doesn’t automatically make an offer exceptional.
We consider the complete purchase, too: the retailer, product condition, warranty, and any conditions attached to the price. For desktop Macs, we also account for the display and accessories you’ll need. Our Mac buying guide and MacBook comparison explain how to choose the right model and configuration.

title: Apple's Smart Glasses Strategy Hinges on Siri and iPhone Apps
content:
Apple plans to unveil its first smart glasses at WWDC in June 2027 and begin shipping them before the end of the year, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In the latest edition of his "Power On" newsletter, Gurman shared new details about the glasses' design, charging system, and Siri features.

Current prototypes of the glasses, internally code-named "N50," are reportedly slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans. Some test units have oval camera openings integrated into the frame without protruding housings. A front light indicates use or charging, while Apple is experimenting with additional privacy features.

FaceTime audio.

Testers can also charge the prototype glasses while wearing them. A flat, three-pin magnetic connector, "roughly the size of a Tic Tac," attaches near the end of the left temple arm. Gurman said it remains unclear whether Apple will use this charging system in the shipping product.

The first model will not display augmented reality imagery. Wearers will interact through ‌Siri‌, which will use the cameras to answer questions about their surroundings.

Planned uses include identifying buildings, suggesting meals based on ingredients in a refrigerator, providing directions, and translating signs and conversations. Apple also intends to support calls, messages, iPhone notifications, calendars, standard and visual reminders, music controls, and smart home controls.

To support the glasses, developers will need to let ‌Siri‌ control specific features in their iPhone apps. Apple envisions tasks such as booking restaurant tables, requesting rides, ordering coffee, shopping, and purchasing movie tickets working on the device.

Developers will not need to create separate apps for the glasses. Their software will run on a paired iPhone, with the two devices working together to fulfill requests. Current plans require a recent iPhone model, with no Android support. The paired phone will compensate for the glasses' limited processing power and memory.

Wi-Fi will allow certain functions outside third-party apps to remain available without a nearby iPhone. Gurman suggested audio playback could theoretically continue over Wi-Fi, although the glasses will not function as a fully independent device.

Internal prototypes purportedly run a reduced version of visionOS 28 and contain a processor derived from older Apple Watch chips. Other custom components handle wireless connectivity and process images as the cameras capture them.

Apple began introducing the necessary ‌Siri‌ controls in this month's first iOS 27.3 beta, enabling more precise control of app actions. Originally demonstrated in 2024, the capability has been rebuilt using newer AI models. Apple plans to release support for its own apps in December, followed by third-party support in 2027.

Apple wants developers to prepare those integrations before the glasses arrive and continues to target a WWDC announcement next year. The company sees access to its existing app ecosystem as a major selling point against rival smart glasses.

The device will also overlap with camera-equipped AirPods, which remain scheduled for launch in late 2027 and will also provide ‌Siri‌ with information about the user's surroundings. The glasses should offer longer battery life and accommodate more sensors, with Apple seeing the potential for them to be worn throughout the day.

Lots of cars from the last decade support CarPlay, but only through a cable plugged into the dash. On a long Thanksgiving drive, that cable is one more thing to untangle every time someone gets back in the car. If you’d rather leave your iPhone in your pocket, try this wireless CarPlay and Android Auto adapter. Through November 15, it costs $89.97 (reg. $149.99) and ships free.
Plug the adapter into the USB port your car already uses for CarPlay, and your phone will connect over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth afterward. This adapter works with 98% of car models from 2016 onward that have wired CarPlay and a touchscreen. Cars with built-in wireless CarPlay won’t work with it, and neither will some BMW, Tesla, Mazda, and Nissan models. Your iPhone needs iOS 10 or later, and three cables come in the box.

title: Top Stories: Apple's New Software Approach, iPhone Duo-Optimized Apps, and More
content:
Apple's wild past few months are finally starting to slow down with the last of the big hardware launches coming this week.


Meanwhile, developers are continuing to optimize their apps for the all-new form factor of the iPhone Duo and Apple looks to shake up its internal iOS and macOS development to give engineers more time to explore and develop new features within the existing update cycles, so read on below for all of the details on these stories and more!

Top Stories

Apple Taking New Approach to Developing iOS 28 and macOS 28

Apple has made a change to its development process for iOS 28, macOS 28, and corresponding software updates, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In his Power On newsletter this week, he said Apple separates development of each year's new operating systems into three major stages. Typically, he said each stage consists of four weeks of coding followed by a four-week "convergence" period where new features are integrated into the operating systems.

This time around, Apple has made a change, extending the coding period of each stage to six weeks and compressing the convergence period to two weeks, giving engineers more time to come up with and explore ideas before having to lock them in. The change could allow Apple to move more quickly on feature development, part of a general shift toward trying to become more nimble under new CEO John Ternus.

'Apple Support Community' Permanently Closing on November 20

Apple this week abruptly announced that the long-running Apple Support Community discussion forums will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20. Effective immediately, the Apple Support Community forums are in a read-only state, with new posts no longer being accepted.


Longtime members of the community were blindsided by the move and left without an opportunity to post farewell messages to others in the community.

Apple Says More Than 100,000 Apps Optimized for iPhone Duo, Here's What's Still Missing

Apple last week announced that more than 100,000 apps have been optimized for the iPhone Duo, delivering full compatibility with the device's inner and outer displays. Despite the volume of apps that have been updated, a number of high-profile apps have yet to be optimized, but more and more are being updated each day.


The new form factor of the iPhone Duo opens up new possibilities for app functionality and layouts, and we've shared several rounds of fun new apps, innovative games and utilities, and more.

Hands-On With Apple's New OLED Touchscreen MacBook Pro, HomeView Smart Home Hub, and Apple TV

Apple's long-rumored MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now in the hands of customers, and we've shared our initial impressions of Apple's first touchscreen Mac.


The touchscreen functionality arrives as part of a new display based on OLED technology, and the machine is significantly lighter than previous models while also delivering a number of other improvements. And yes, the long-lost lighted Apple logo on the lid has made a return!

HomeView smart home hub and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K box.

Apple Store Subscription Sign-Up Controversy Exposed

In a series of YouTube videos shared over the past few weeks, electronics technician and consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann has exposed a controversy in which some Apple Store employees have allegedly signed up customers for auto-renewing subscription trials for Apple One and other services without their informed consent.


Apple has historically tracked the "services attach rate" for retail employees, leading some to feel pressure to push the limits on signing customers up for trials without getting clear permission.

Apple has recently removed the attach rate metric for retail employees, though the company has said it is because the metric is less relevant for the holiday season when users are more often buying as gifts rather than for themselves, but the timing of the change is certainly convenient given the recent publicity.

Apple Releases iOS 27.2.1 With Bug Fixes

Apple this week released iOS 27.2.1 and related updates, delivering a number of security-related updates and other unspecified bug fixes. tvOS 27.2.1 also arrived on Friday, bringing Siri AI to 2nd- and 3rd-generation Apple TV 4K boxes.


The releases come as much more substantial 27.3 updates remain early in beta testing ahead of public releases next month.

title: HomeView Tidbits: Mirror, Sleep Timer, and Other Details
content:
Apple's HomeView is out today, and we're finally learning all the little details about the new hub. We've rounded up a list of tidbits for those setting up a HomeView or thinking about getting one.


Sunglasses

Apple says the HomeView probably won't recognize you if you have your face covered, including when wearing sunglasses. If HomeView isn't identifying you, Apple suggests removing anything that would block the camera from seeing your face.

The HomeView's screen needs to be angled toward your face, you need to be centered in the frame and closest to the camera if other people are around, and the HomeView can't be blocked by overhanging shelves and cabinets. Apple says the HomeView needs front-facing, even light.
Mirror

There's a "Mirror" in the HomeView Control Center that lets you use the camera to see yourself. There's an option to turn on an edge light for face illumination, along with 1x and 2x zoom.
Guest Controls

The HomeView owner has multiple options for what guests can access.

 	
Safari can be turned on or off, or adult websites can be blocked.

 	
By default, guests can use Siri for general knowledge, writing help, and math help, but ‌Siri‌ features can be turned off.

 	
Explicit content can be turned on or off.

 	
There's an option to choose which Apple Music subscription supplies music for an unrecognized user.


Wi-Fi/Cellular

The HomeView authenticates people through face recognition and by making sure their iOS device is nearby, recently unlocked, and on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView. If there's a Wi-Fi outage, Apple says cellular can also be used to unlock personal content as long as it's in the same location and was recently on the Wi-Fi network.
Sleep Timer

You can set a sleep timer on HomeView to pause whatever media is playing when the timer goes off.
No Buttons

There is no button to turn the HomeView on or off, or restart it. It can be restarted from the Settings app or by briefly unplugging it.
Logins

You can log into websites and apps using your iPhone, similar to how the Apple TV works.
Notifications

The HomeView only has notifications for phone calls and home devices, with an option to toggle on critical notifications. There are no other notification settings or options.
Liquid Glass

The transparency of the Liquid Glass interface can be adjusted from clear to opaque like on iPhone, iPad, and Mac.
Personal Data Lockouts

If someone tries to repeatedly access personal content on HomeView that needs authentication, facial recognition via the camera is disabled and you'll need to prove identity with a registered device.

title: Update: Microsoft offers explanation for day-long Internet outage
content:
Macworld





Whether you’re using a Mac, iPhone, or – shudder – a PC, a major Microsoft outage has disrupted Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services worldwide. The problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued overnight into Friday, affecting businesses, schools and public services.
Microsoft said a server process had become overwhelmed, reducing capacity. Recovery proved difficult because some servers became unresponsive again as traffic returned. Features that depend on Exchange Online were particularly affected, although not every function within each Microsoft service stopped working.
A look at Downdetector and ThousandEyes Outages also showed complaints involving unrelated platforms. However, those reports don’t establish that every service was down or that they shared Microsoft’s underlying problem. Amazon told Macworld that AWS was operating normally. Some users also reported problems with iMessage, although Apple’s System Status page showed no corresponding outage at the time.
Microsoft reported signs of recovery as it restarted affected infrastructure and managed traffic, but had not provided a confirmed time for full restoration. The company had not established a final root cause and said there was no indication that malicious activity was responsible.
You can track the Microsoft service health here, and we’ll keep this article updated as we learn more.


Update November 14, 4:17 a.m. GMT / November 13, 11:17 p.m. ET: Final restoration confirmed
Microsoft confirmed that the Microsoft 365 outage had been resolved. The company claims the outage was caused by a technical problem associated with a network-capacity upgrade. 
Recovery continues to be monitored. 


						

							


Update 8:55 pm GMT / 3:55 pm ET: Network change blamed
Microsoft has apologized for the outage as it works to restore all systems to normal: “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”


						

							


Update 11:45 am GMT / 6.45 am ET: Recovery underway
Microsoft says it has completed recovery actions in Asia-Pacific and this recovery work is being extended to other regions, as per the Guardian’s live blog. 


						

							


Update 10:15 am GMT / 5.15 am ET: The U.K. has woken up to the Microsoft outage
Microsoft’s service disruption continued into Friday, November 13, affecting Outlook email and Microsoft 365 features that depend on Exchange Online. 
The disruption has affected NHS communications, with reports of NHS trusts, including Evelina London, a children’s healthcare provider, unable to send or receive emails. 
Elsewhere, police forces have confirmed that some online reporting forms could be affected, but their ability to answer and respond to 999 and 101 calls had not been compromised. 
Schools have also reported communication problems and asked parents to telephone rather than email their child’s school.
Microsoft’s Friday morning advisory, via the University of Pennsylvania’s Microsoft incident-report feed, says most core Teams calling, meetings and messaging functionality is unaffected, although calendar and other email-dependent features can fail.
Microsoft reported early signs of stabilization on Friday morning, but said capacity had not returned to normal and recovery remained uneven.


						

							


Update 9:45 pm ET: “Positive results” 
Microsoft reported “seeing positive results” with its efforts to correct the outage as it restarted affected infrastructure and brought servers back into service in isolation.


						

							


Update 4:39 pm ET: AWS is normal 
An Amazon spokesperson reached out to Macworld to let us know that AWS is functioning normally and has been all day. 
Any disruptions today would have to be caused by something else.


						

							


Update 2:00 pm ET: The whole Internet is having major issues right now
Whether you’re using a Mac, iPhone, or – shudder – a PC, you may be having trouble accessing Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services.
Downdetector and ThousandEyes Outages are recording widespread reports of connectivity problems. Users have also reported issues with unrelated platforms, although those reports do not establish that every service is down or that they share the same underlying cause.
Some users are reporting problems with Apple services, including iMessage, but Apple’s System Status page shows no corresponding outage at the time of writing.
OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported disruption to the tools that connect their AI assistants to Microsoft 365. For ChatGPT users who connect Microsoft services, this could interrupt tasks that depend on retrieving information from those services.
The cause and expected restoration time remain unclear. We’ll update this live blog as providers confirm more information.
creator: Macworld

title: Microsoft 365 Outage Resolving After Nearly 24 Hours
content:
The ongoing Microsoft 365 outage is resolving after nearly 24 hours. The company said the underlying issue has been fixed and it is seeing "broad recovery and stability" across its services as it works to restore access to customers.


The Microsoft 365 downtime started at approximately 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday. Customers could not access their Outlook email or use some features in Teams and Copilot. Exchange accounts in Apple Mail were also affected. Most calling, meeting, and messaging functions stayed online, but some users ran into errors scheduling meetings or adding calendar entries.

Businesses, educational institutions, and governments worldwide were impacted by the outage.

Microsoft apologized for the outage and said it was unrelated to a cyberattack or AI agents. It was caused by an issue introduced in an earlier network capacity upgrade. Microsoft said it will give a full incident report after completing a review.
We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.

This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.


Just over two weeks ago, Microsoft announced plans to eliminate thousands of jobs. The company offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 people, or a quarter of its global workforce, presumably to cut costs while its AI spending grows.

Service Health Status page still says some services may be unavailable at the current time.

title: iPhone Duo Survives 450,000 Folds, but Hinge is Weakening
content:
For the last three weeks, CNET has been stress testing the iPhone Duo's hinge on a livestream. After over 451,000 folds, the hinge is showing signs of wear.



CNET says the hinge started feeling looser at the 390,000-fold point, and by 440,300 folds, there was enough of a shift in the mechanism that the screen didn't open in full before the machine closed it again, and there was no distinctive snap. It is 5 to 10 degrees from the fully open state and can be opened fully by hand.
The wire we use to open the phone screen would withdraw before the screen was in the fully open position, but it would then sort of "coast" the rest of the way down. But between 12:30 and 1 a.m. this morning, around 440,300 folds, the screen would no longer have time to open all the way before the Fold-a-Phone caused it to close again.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ hasn't been removed from the folding machine, and the test is continuing. CNET says the device is still operational and maintaining other screen positions, with no signs of cracking or other failure.

The site plans to continue folding the ‌iPhone Duo‌ until it hits predetermined failure conditions that include loss of power, sensors failing to detect the screen properly, and screen blackout.

Apple hasn't shared the results of ‌iPhone Duo‌ hinge testing it likely did internally, or given an estimated fold lifespan.

OLED panels sourced from Samsung Display, and Samsung's screens have undergone certified third-party fold testing. The display used for the Galaxy Z Fold7 passed a 500,000-fold durability test. Apple probably isn't using an off-the-shelf Samsung display, but CNET's testing already suggests the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s ‌OLED‌ panel is on track to match.

The combination of the display and the strength of Apple's hinge design will determine lifespan. At around 450,000 folds, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ would last over a decade at 100 folds per day.

CNET's livestream will continue until the ‌iPhone Duo‌ fails. The livestream runs on weekdays from 10 a.m. Pacific until 2 p.m. Pacific.

Apple

Apple

What it’s about: Deadline reports that Apple has won the bidding war for rights to a movie about the storied cyclist Lance Armstrong.

When you can watch: The Lance Armstrong biopic does not yet have a title or release date.
Foster the Snowman
What it’s about: Per Deadline, Apple out-bid Netflix and MGM for this holiday high-concept movie about a snowman that comes alive, and will go through every stage of life in just 72 hours. The childless couple who act as his “parents” go through every parenting milestone in just three days.
Important names: No stars are yet attached. The film will be directed by Hikari.

Once and Again

Important names: This project is early in product and has no director or stars attached yet.

When you can watch: Neuromancer is in production now but does not yet have a release date.

A Deadline report says Apple is developing an hour-long drama series about Barris as both Gong Show host and CIA assassin.

When you can watch: This series has no release date yet.  
Dolly

Bride

Important names: The film will star Scarlett Johansson and will be directed by Sebastián Lelio.
When you can watch: No release date yet.

Important names: It will be executive produced by Alex Williamson, and the series producer is Sam Hodgson.

What it’s about: According to Variety, this is to be a “spy movie with romance set in Africa” but little else is known about the nascent project. The report says it’s early in production. 
Important names: The film will star Idris Elba and is produced by Simon Kinberg and Audrey Chon.
When you can watch: No release date yet.
Hedy Lamarr series
What it’s about: According to The Hollywood Reporter, it’s an eight-episode series about the 1930s and 40s actress and inventor Hedy Lamarr (whose frequency-hopping radio technology is still the basis for many modern wireless communications).
Important names: Gal Gadot is set to star as Lamarr, with a script written by Sarah Treem.

What it’s about: Apple has struck an overall deal with The Maurice Sendak Foundation to produce shows or series based on the author’s works for children. The most famous of these, by far, is Where the Wild Things Are.
Important names: Apple is working with longtime Sendak collaborator Arthur Yorinks and his production studio Night Kitchen Studios.

title: Binance warns of iOS 27 flaw that could expose ‘private keys and login credentials’
content:
Macworld





Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has issued a warning that recent versions of iOS have a security vulnerability that can put Apple devices “at risk.” The vulnerability can be found in iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2. Binance states that the vulnerability allows malicious software to “read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem.”
However, the vulnerability can only be exploited if the malicious software was installed outside of the App Store. In other words, the malicious app has to be installed by sideloading or by a manually signed iOS App Store Package. That’s unlikely to happen outside of the EU, where Apple allows alternative app marketplaces and installation of apps outside of the App Store. 
The current version of iOS is 27.2.1, which was released on November 9, but it is not clear if that update includes a security fix that addresses the issue. Because the issue involves an unauthorized method of software installation, Apple may not address the issue immediately.
How to protect your iPhone from malware
Sideloading apps increases your chances of security risk. Software that is available on the App Store has been vetted for security issues. To minimize the chances of inadvertently installing malware, do not sideload apps on your iPhone and only use apps from the App Store. If you do sideload apps, understand that you have increased your risk.
The easiest task to perform to secure your iPhone is to update the operating system. iOS can be updated in the Settings app by tapping General > Software Update. Apple also has a separate method for installing immediate security patches called Background Security Improvements. It is located in Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom to find Background Security Improvements. Macworld has a list of tips for keeping your iPhone secure.

HomeView software delivers powerful, personalized experiences to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage your smart home. It features a conversational Siri AI that helps you find what you need and get things done. And with multiuser recognition, customizable faces, and deep Apple ecosystem integration, up to six members of your household get content and controls tailored just for them.

Siri AI

A more capable and conversational version of Siri that helps you find what you need and get more done

Personal context understanding draws on your Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to help you find what you're looking for, like that recipe your mother emailed you

Broad world knowledge lets you ask questions about virtually any topic and get a detailed answer

Rich content discovery makes it easy to find new music and podcasts using natural language

HomeView and Siri AI on HomeView are available in English, and require your paired iPhone or iPad to be set to the same English variant¹,²



Entertainment

Apple Music lets you enjoy your favorite songs with animated lyrics and Spatial Audio support, alongside easy search and browse capabilities

Podcasts lets you enjoy audio and video shows with transcripts and personalized recommendations

Apple TV, Apple News, and Audiobooks let you use your iPhone to enjoy your favorite shows, catch up on daily audio stories, or get lost in a good book

Supported third-party audio and video apps installed on your iPhone automatically appear on HomeView

Multiroom audio allows you to play and control music in sync across multiple HomeView, HomePod, and AirPlay speakers



Connection

FaceTime makes it easy to connect with loved ones hands-free, using Center Stage to keep you perfectly framed even as you move around the room

Messages lets you easily read and reply to texts using Siri, the onscreen keyboard, or Tapback

Intercom allows you to broadcast messages across your home, to specific rooms, or to personal Apple devices

Safari lets you browse the web and includes a new Cooking experience that auto-detects supported recipes, reformatting them with step-by-step instructions and inline timers

Find My lets you view the location of friends and family, or locate misplaced Apple devices and AirTags

Handoff makes it easy to seamlessly move audio, video, websites, or calls directly from your iPhone to HomeView



Home Control

Home Modular face offers a concise, glanceable look at your home accessories

Home Camera face allows you to livestream up to nine simultaneous camera feeds

Home app gives you a dedicated dashboard to control accessories and activate scenes across your entire house

Home hub capabilities keep you connected to your HomeKit and Matter accessories, allow you to control your home while away, and enable automations

Sound Recognition detects the sounds of smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and alerts you on personal devices like your iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch



Personalized Experiences

Customizable faces let you personalize your space with curated photos, modular home controls, and playful animations like Snoopy

Seamless recognition identifies up to six different users by face and voice, instantly displaying their specific Home Screen layout, widgets, and personal content

Personal content³ like Messages and Calendar is designed to stay private and be displayed when an enrolled user is recognized, and their recently unlocked iPhone or iPad is present and on the same network

Guest experience lets unrecognized people play media and control smart home accessories without accessing a user's personal content

title: Apple Says HomeView Sets New Record in Design-Focused Interview
content:
TechRadar's Jacob Krol interviewed Apple's Vice President of Hardware Engineering Matthew Costello about Apple's all-new HomeView smart home display, which is available starting today. The discussion was largely focused on the HomeView's design, with Costello touching on the device achieving a display-related record for Apple products.


Specifically, the HomeView's display brightness can automatically go down to just 0.3 nits, which is a record low for any Apple product. This ultra-low brightness makes the HomeView especially ideal for a bedside table at night. 

"I really love the fact that this is the lowest light performance we've ever engineered into a product, so it's down to 0.3 nits," said Costello.

"So officially, I represent the most dim product ever inside of Apple," he quipped.

For comparison, some other Apple products like the latest iPhones and iPad mini are advertised as having a minimum 1-nit display brightness.

HomeView's maximum display brightness is 500 nits.

Unsurprisingly, Costello said the HomeView is designed for the home (truly shocking) and Siri AI.

"It really was constructed around Siri," he said. 

"We really custom-built this user interface for the home, so the apps and experiences that matter most in the home setting are really front and center," he added.

"There's no logging in, logging out, which is super cool. It recognizes you and your information, and when you step away, it's gone."

content:
Macworld





Whether you’re a Mac desktop or MacBook owner, there’s nothing quite like finding that keyboard that fits perfectly within your setup.
A keyboard, just as with picking the best mice for Mac, is a very personal choice. After all, you’re likely to be pressing its various keys and twirling its dials for hours each day, and that makes getting the investment right all that much more important.
Best Mac Keyboards fully tested
We have all sorts of Mac keyboards in this round-up, including Apple’s default Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and the cheaper, and still-on-sale Magic Keyboard. We have some keyboards with customizable keys and dedicated apps, and wired keyboards (for those fed up with searching for new batteries every few weeks) as well as ergonomic solutions to help you avoid RSI, and some pretty stylish offerings that give Apple a run for its money.
We also look at Hall Effect options that use magnetic sensors to detect key presses, full-size offerings and compact board. Here are our favorite keyboards for Mac users, many of which cost a lot less than Apple’s. Read on to find the Mac compatible keyboard that’s best for you.
You can also use Bluetooth keyboards with iPads, so expect to see some good options here if you are an iPad user, or take a look at our Best iPad Keyboards roundup.

Apple sells four models of its Magic Keyboard, and some are more magical than others despite looking similar. There are two sizes (one with numeric keypad and navigation keys, and a smaller, more portable model without these extra keys). If your desk space is limited or you often travel with your keyboard, the 11-inch version makes more sense than the 16.5-inch keyboard.
Keyboard type: Slim
Size options: Compact, Full
Colors: White, Black (full-size only)
Aside from size, the two different models are differentiated by the inclusion of a Touch ID key, which works only with Macs that have an M-series Apple Silicon processor (post 2020). If your Mac is old enough to still be running an Intel chip, go for the non-Touch ID model. Only the Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and Numeric Keypad is available with black keys; the others are all-white affairs. rather cheekily, Apple charges an extra 20 buck for the black version. Each is available in nearly 20 different language versions. English speakers can choose between US or British English.
The basic design of the two keyboards hasn’t actually changed that much, with the same slimline design and month-long battery life as their predecessors. At $149, the smaller Magic Keyboard With Touch ID is priced at quite a premium for the Touch ID sensor. And, like the standard Magic Keyboard, it feels rather cramped, with a small Space bar and cursor keys. The lack of ‘travel’ (the up and down movement of the keys as you press them) also makes the keyboard feel a bit lifeless for people who type a lot and need a bit more tactile feedback when they’re typing up a storm—they should consider one of the mechanical keyboards reviewed below. Then again, you might feel that your fingers have to do less ‘work’ compressing the key. 
The key feature of these keyboards, though, is the Touch ID sensor, which sits by the F12 button on the top row of Function keys. This works just like the Touch ID sensors on the MacBook. You’ll see a Touch ID panel appear in System Preferences when you first connect the keyboard. This allows you to store up to three fingerprints, which you can use to unlock your Mac, or to make secure payments on the Apple Store, or other online stores that support Apple Pay.

The K950 is just as versatile as its more expensive counterpart, though. And, like the MX Keys S, the K950 includes a special set of buttons that allow you to pair it with three different devices and quickly switch between them, including Macs, iPads, Windows PCs, Chrome and Linux. Most of the Function keys work with the Mac automatically, but you can also use Logitech’s Options+ app to reprogram the keys to suit the apps that you work with most.

Apple’s keyboards are a bit confusing, with two generations of keyboards available, and each generation offering two different keyboards, with or without a numeric keypad.
The older generation of Magic Keyboards is still available, and is now intended primarily for use with older Macs that have Intel processors. These older keyboards lack the Touch ID sensor that is available with the two new keyboards that Apple launched in the summer of 2021.
Touch ID and some of the other features of the new keyboards don’t work with Intel-based Macs, so if your Mac has an Intel processor then these older keyboards are the best options available from Apple—although, of course, there are plenty of other keyboards available from other manufacturers, which we review here as well.
The smaller Magic Keyboard can be expensive at $99/£99, but its elegant slimline design started a trend for ‘low-profile’ keyboards that many other manufacturers now follow too.
The aluminum body does feel quite sturdy, but the slimline design means that the keys don’t ‘travel’ very well, so speedy typists might prefer a larger keyboard that is actually designed to do some proper work rather than just looking pretty.
The Space Bar and the little set of navigation keys in the lower-right corner of the keyboard are also rather small and fiddly. To be fair, though, the compact little keyboard does squeeze in quite a few useful features, with the top row of Function keys providing controls for brightness, volume and playing music.
The Magic Keyboard works as a standard Bluetooth keyboard, and Apple says that its rechargeable battery will last for about a month at a time. Note that some models have a Lightning port rather than USB-C for charging.
And, of course, there’s the larger version, called the Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad ($129/£129). This is also quite expensive but adds a numeric keypad for people who need to do a bit of serious number crunching every now and then. This keyboard also has a larger set of navigation keys, which is very useful for scrolling through long documents or web pages, and an additional set of navigation keys that allow you to quickly jump to the top or bottom of a document.
The larger keyboard layout also means that there’s room for some additional Function keys too, going right up to F19 (rather than F12 for the smaller Magic Keyboard). It’s a shame, though, that the options in the macOS for programming your own keyboard shortcuts are fairly limited, so power users might prefer to use a third-party utility such as USB OverDrive or HotKey App, to make full use of these extra Function keys. This larger keyboard has the same month-long battery life as the smaller Magic Keyboard, although it’s showing its age a little as (surprisingly) its charging cable still has a USB-A connector.
You can find the best prices for Apple Keyboards and Mice in our deals round-up.
How to pick the best keyboard 
Choosing the right keyboard is a personal decision that can significantly impact your daily comfort and productivity, whether you’re typing, gaming, or doing creative work. Key factors to consider include the keyboard’s primary use, its physical design, and the technology inside its keys.
Before diving into specific models, consider what you need from a keyboard. Your choice will depend on a combination of feel, features, and function.
Typing Experience and Comfort: The feel of the keys under your fingers is one of the most critical aspects. This includes key travel (the distance a key moves when pressed), the force required to register a keystroke, and the overall sound and tactile feedback. Some users prefer the deep, satisfying feedback of mechanical keyboards, while others favor the quiet, low-profile feel of membrane or scissor-switch models. Ergonomics also play a huge role; features like an adjustable typing angle, a built-in wrist rest, or even a split layout can help prevent discomfort and repetitive strain injuries.
Size and Layout: Keyboards come in various sizes. Full-size layouts include a numeric keypad, which is essential for anyone who frequently works with numbers. More compact options, such as tenkeyless (TKL), 75%, and 65% layouts, omit the number pad to save desk space and are often preferred by gamers or those with smaller workstations. The layout also affects the size and placement of important keys like the Shift and arrow keys, which can impact your typing habits. Familiar with an Apple keyboard lay out? A PC layout is very different, with various keys located in different positions and the Command and Alt/Option key switched.
Connectivity and Compatibility: You’ll need to decide between a wired or wireless keyboard. Wired keyboards offer a reliable connection without battery concerns, while wireless models provide a cleaner, untethered setup. Many wireless keyboards can connect via Bluetooth or a 2.4GHz USB dongle/receiver, with some offering the ability to pair with and switch between multiple devices, which is great for multitasking across a laptop, tablet, and phone. Some find using a 2.4GHz receiver is more responsive than Bluetooth, so this is often favored by gamers. Many USB dongles, however, are USB-A, and there’s no USB-A port on any modern Apple product so you might need an adapter. Also, ensure the keyboard is compatible with your operating system, whether it’s macOS, Windows, or both. Some keyboards include swappable keycaps and a switch to toggle between layouts. 
Language: It goes without saying that if you will want a keyboard that matches the keyboard layout common in your country. Especially if you aren’t an English speaker. 
Customization and Special Features: Many modern keyboards, especially mechanical ones, offer extensive customization. This can range from remapping keys and creating macros to swapping out the physical keycaps and switches (hot-swapping). Other features to look for include backlighting (for typing in low light), dedicated media controls or volume knobs, and specialized software for adjusting settings.
Mechanical vs Membrane Keyboards
The most significant distinction in keyboard technology is between mechanical and membrane models. This choice fundamentally shapes the typing experience.
Mechanical Keyboards: Praised for their durability, tactile feedback, and customizability, mechanical keyboards feature an individual physical switch under each key. This construction provides a more precise and consistent feel, with switches rated for tens of millions of keystrokes . They are highly popular with typists and gamers alike.
Switch Types: The feel of a mechanical keyboard is determined by its switches. Common types include linear (smooth, no bump), tactile (a noticeable bump mid-press), and clicky (a bump accompanied by an audible click). Some advanced keyboards feature Hall Effect or magnetic switches, which use electromagnetic fields to actuate keys, offering adjustable actuation points and enhanced durability.
Customization: A major draw for mechanical keyboards is the ability to customize them. Many models are “hot-swappable,” meaning you can easily change the switches without soldering to achieve your desired typing feel . You can also replace the keycaps with different materials, colors, or profiles.
Membrane Keyboards: These are the most common type of keyboard, often found in laptops and budget-friendly desktop models . They use a rubber or silicone layer under the keys that registers a keystroke when pressed down. While quieter and more affordable, they often provide a “spongy” or less precise feel and have a shorter lifespan compared to their mechanical counterparts . However, some high-quality membrane keyboards use a “scissor-switch” mechanism, which adds stability and provides a firmer, more responsive feel, similar to many modern laptop keyboards.
Finding the right keyboard for your needs
A keyboard is a very personal choice, and there’s no single “best” option for everyone.
For Office Work and Typing: If you type for long hours, prioritize comfort and ergonomics. A full-size keyboard with a number pad can boost productivity . Mechanical keyboards with tactile switches are often favored for their satisfying feedback, but a high-quality, quiet scissor-switch keyboard like the Logitech MX Keys S is also an excellent choice for a general-purpose office keyboard and is much quieter.
For Gaming: Gamers often prioritize speed and responsiveness. Keyboards with low latency, a high polling rate, and features like adjustable actuation or “rapid trigger” mode can provide a competitive edge . Compact TKL or 75% layouts are popular because they leave more room for mouse movement. Linear switches are often preferred for their smooth, quick action.
For Creatives and Customization Enthusiasts: Creatives may benefit from keyboards with special features like programmable dials or macro keys, such as the Logitech Craft . For those who love to tinker, a hot-swappable mechanical keyboard from a brand like Keychron offers endless possibilities for customization, from the switches and keycaps to the case material and internal sound-dampening foam.
Ultimately, the best way to choose a keyboard is to understand your own preferences for feel, sound, and features. From there, you can explore the different types of keyboard layouts, learn about the nuances of mechanical switch types, or compare the benefits of wired versus wireless keyboards.
