title: If your old printer stopped working with macOS 27, there’s an easy fix
content:
Macworld





Printers may be one of the most hated devices in tech, but even in 2026, they’re a necessary part of our setups. We need them for specific, usually time-sensitive tasks, and when they don’t work, it can be a major pain.
For a lot of Mac users upgrading to macOS 27 Golden Gate, including me, that’s exactly what happened. While we’re used to some things needing updates or permissions to work after updating to a new version of macOS, Golden Gate caused more problems than usual, and some of the devices that you’ve depended on for years might have suddenly stopped working—including some Brother and Canon printers. If you’re like me, it might take a few weeks to notice because, well, you’re probably not printing things all that often. But when you do, it’s important, and you need it to work.
You can try to find a newer driver, but depending on the age of your printer, there’s a good chance you won’t be able to find one that’s been updated in a while. And if you try deleting your printer and adding it as a new device, it probably won’t be found either.
The problem lies with Rosetta, the background process that automatically translates Intel-based apps for use with Apple Silicon. It’s been silently running in the background ever since macOS Big Sur on the first M1 Macs. However, Apple removed its installation with macOS 27 Golden Gate as it prepares for a world without Intel apps when macOS 28 arrives next year.
Since many printers stick around for years, some very popular models relied on Rosetta to communicate with Apple Silicon Macs. Without Rosetta, that can’t happen with an old Intel-based driver. But there’s an easy fix. Rosetta actually still exists on your Mac; it just needs to be turned on. 
How to install Rosetta
Open the Terminal app. It is located in Applications > Utilities, but you can also press Command-spacebar, type “Terminal” and press Return.
 In Terminal, at the prompt, enter: softwareupdate --install-rosetta
Press Return.
The app will ask you to agree to the software license agreement. Assuming you do, press the letter “A” and hit Return.
It’ll take a moment to install. Once the installation is done you can quit Terminal.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Your printer should now work, though you might need to restart the job that failed. If that doesn’t work, restart your Mac.
The bad news is that unless Apple changes its mind, you’ll need to get a new printer or a different workaround when macOS 28 arrives next year. But until then, happy printing.

service health page says affected users may have trouble opening mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop, and mobile. Messages may also be delayed.

title: HomeView has one big problem: The iPad
content:
Macworld





HomeView is Apple’s new attempt to compete with Amazon and Google in the smart home market. It only arrived in stores today, but it’s already shaping up to be a hit. Its design, which is somewhat reminiscent of a smaller iMac G4, is cute, and it runs an operating system based on iOS. But HomeView’s biggest problem is that there’s already another Apple product that can do most of the same things.
The main purpose of HomeView is to function as a HomeKit hub. But because it’s an Apple device, it also comes with some of the company’s most popular apps preinstalled. It lets you answer FaceTime calls, play songs on Apple Music, or even check your calendar with Siri AI. All of this comes packed into a device that costs $299, not exactly cheap, but relatively affordable for a new Apple product in 2026. But when even the cheapest iPad can do everything HomeView does and more, Apple’s new smart home hub starts to seem quite expensive for what it does.
The iPad is already a great smart home display
Many Apple users had been eagerly awaiting the company’s first smart home hub. That’s no surprise, given the vast market for HomeKit accessories. But the thing is, iPads were already fulfilling that role for many users already in the Apple ecosystem without even realizing it. 
Think about most of the things you’re most likely to do with a HomeView — check the weather, control the lights, send a message, play music. You can already do all of these things with an iPad without having to buy a new device. In fact, many Apple users have already turned an old iPad into a de facto smart home display just by placing it on a stand.

				
					

				
			
The new OLED iPad mini has a bigger screen and more capabilities than the HomeView.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Granted, there are important differences between the two. The iPad wasn’t designed to be a smart hub and lacks some of HomeView’s really useful features, such as an always-on display and private multi-user support. Still, in other areas, the iPad ends up being much more versatile. The iPad can run pretty much any app from the App Store, while there’s no mechanism for installing apps on HomeView. And even the iPad mini has a larger canvas than the HomeView for widgets.
In terms of design, the iPad also has some advantages. The entry-level model features an 11-inch screen, compared to the HomeView’s 7-inch screen. Plus, the iPad has a built-in battery, so you can move it freely around your home. With HomeView, you have to think about where to place it and leave it there. 
Not only that, but you need to decide whether you want HomeView with its base or wall mount — there’s no way to switch between the two. With the iPad, you can. Sure, the HomeView has better speakers and a design that looks nicer sitting on a kitchen counter. But is that really worth giving up everything else?
The things HomeView does best
To be fair, it’s not that HomeView doesn’t have any benefits over the iPad. The first is Apple Intelligence — if you buy the cheapest iPad available today, it lacks even the most basic of Apple’s native AI features. HomeView is powered by the A18 chip from the iPhone 16, so it works with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. It can answer more complex questions and even pull contextual information from your iPhone. The entry-level iPad, on the other hand, is still stuck with the old Siri. However, it’s only a matter of time before the base-model iPad gets a chip capable of running Siri AI.
But there’s another feature that might be even more important: multi-user support. Unlike the iPad, which was designed to be a personal device, HomeView can be used by up to six people in the same household. This is a must-have feature if you don’t want other people in your house snooping on your messages or photos. 
HomeView uses a Face ID-like facial recognition system to display each user’s personal data. Each person has their own Home Screen, widgets, and app content. From that perspective, HomeView makes a lot more sense as a smart hub than the single-user iPad.

				
					

				
			
HomeView’s biggest advantage is its app-less simplicity and muilti-user support

Foundry




HomeView vs. iPad: Which one to choose?
Don’t get me wrong, I do like the idea of the HomeView. It’s a great addition to Apple’s ecosystem, especially for those who have a lot of HomeKit stuff at home. Having a dedicated screen that anyone in the house can use is a nice feature that’s not really available on any other Apple device, and unlike an iPad, the HomeView is designed to be always available. You don’t have to worry about charging it, finding where you left it, or unlocking it every time you want to turn on the lights.
But I still think it’s hard to justify its price given all its limitations. Yes, an entry-level iPad costs $150 more, but it also does a lot more. It can serve as your smart home display and also function just like any other tablet, with a vast ecosystem of apps available. If you already have an old iPad at home, that’s even better. You just need to buy a stand for it. If not, a refurbished 11th-generation iPad costs almost the same as a HomeView.
I don’t think HomeView is a bad product, and it’s actually cool to see Apple getting more involved in the smart home market. But the first generation seems to have too many limitations for its price. So for most users like me, an iPad will likely remain the first choice for some people when it comes to their smart home hub.

title: Best MacBook Neo accessories: Chargers, hubs, stands and more
content:
Macworld





The MacBook Neo, Apple’s entry-level laptop officially announced in early March 2026, is a sensation, bringing the Mac to a whole new market with its low price but surprisingly powerful specs and features. For just $699 you get the full Mac experience in a premium aluminum 13-inch laptop with FaceTime HD camera, speakers, mic and two USB-C ports.
Compared to similarly priced Windows laptops and iPads with keyboards, the MacBook Neo offers superior build quality, performance, and storage capacity—for hundreds of dollars less than any previous Mac laptop.
We’ve outlined some of the small compromises that Apple has made to get to that ultra-keen price point, but most of these technicalities won’t bother the target audience at that great deal of a price tag.
That’s not to say that the MacBook Neo is perfect—otherwise why would the MacBook Air and Pro exist? For not a whole lot of extra outlay you can make the MacBook Neo an even better product and part of your digital lifestyle with these accessories. Here we list some of our favorite Mac accessories that we think every MacBook Neo owner should purchase or at least put on their wish list.
MacBook Neo limitations and solutions
Here are some of the limitations of the MacBook Neo that you can solve with the accessories in this guide. 
Slow 20W charger: Buy a faster charger
Only two USB-C ports: Buy a USB-C hub
One slow 480Mbps port: Buy a USB-C hub
Single external display support: Buy a DisplayLink dock
Small screen for desk use: Buy an external screen

				
					

				
			
Satechi




Essential MacBook Neo accessory 1: A charger
Apple ships the MacBook Neo with a 20-watt (20W) Power Adapter (unless you’re in the U.K. or E.U., where–tough luck–you’ll get just a charging cable and no actual charger). At just 20W, it’s a pretty low-powered adapter to be honest. In fact, it’s now hard to find a charger rated that low, with 30W or 45W increasingly the minimum output.
If you’re in a hurry for power, you’ll want something more capable than Apple’s puny 20W adapter. While Apple doesn’t list fast charging in the Neo’s tech specs, in our own Neo charging tests we found it does charge faster when paired with a more powerful charger.
Charging speed is largely determined by power output. The more watts available, the faster a device can charge—up to its maximum supported input. For example, you can plug a 140W charger into an iPhone, but it won’t charge any faster than it would with a 35W adapter as the Neo’s max input is 30W. A 30W charger will be faster than the 20W but a little more powerful supply will get through any latency. We recommend at least a 35W charger. Better still, buy a much more powerful charger with multiple ports so you can charge more than just your Neo with it.
We’ve chosen two alternative chargers to consider: a compact 45W single-port model and a 65W multiport charger. For more options, see our roundup of the best USB-C chargers for MacBook for even more choice.

Latest security updates: Apple released macOS Golden Gate 27.2.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.3, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 on November 9, 2026
Which version of macOS can my Mac run?
Apple releases a new version of the Mac operating system every year—but the newest version of the Mac operating system does not support every Mac. Each year more and more Macs fall off the compatibility list and are unable to be updated to take advantage of the latest features.

How long do Macs last?
Can I install an older OS on my Mac?
Officially, the operating system that was available on your Mac at the time that you bought it is the oldest version of macOS that can run on that Mac. It’s likely that an older OS won’t include the necessary drivers for the hardware on newer Macs. For this reason, it is unlikely that you will be able to install an older version of macOS on a new Mac—but you can take a look at how to install old versions of macOS or OS X for other Macs. Owners of Macs with M-series chips (sometimes referred to as Apple Silicon) won’t be able to run older versions of macOS that weren’t designed for Apple Silicon Macs which use a different architecture, known as ARM, instead of x86.
But it may not just be a case of wanting to know if your Mac can run the newest operating system. You might also want to know if it is possible to downgrade your Mac to an older version of macOS and need to know the oldest version of macOS you can use. You’ll also find that information below. You can also see a complete list of all the different versions of macOS and Mac OS X. Not sure which Mac you own? Check our article about how to identify your Mac.

title: Apple Explains How HomeView Keeps Camera Data Private
content:
Apple today shared an in-depth look at how it's using Secure Exclaves to protect camera and microphone data on the HomeView, iPhone 18 Pro, and other products.


Apple describes Secure Exclaves as compartmentalized runtimes that process camera and microphone data while isolated from the rest of the operating system. Data processed in Secure Exclaves is not available to the rest of the OS, apps, or Apple, but processing can take advantage of the full application processor. Secure Exclaves power sensitive features involving video and audio feeds:

 	
HomeView - The HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to identify up to six people in a home. The exclave also protects the LED camera indicator on the device.

 	
Siri Recap and Live Rewind - Record ambient sound for conversation recaps or to caption the last 15 seconds of someone speaking.

 	
iPhone 18 Pro/iPhone Duo - Protects the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌, Pro Max, and Duo on-screen camera and microphone indicators. Also works with "Hey Siri" to protect voice data.

 	
MacBook Neo - Protects the MacBook Neo camera indicator.


Apple uses the HomeView as an example of how Secure Exclaves work. The device performs passive minimal visual processing continually to detect whether a person is in its field of view. The HomeView sends a continuous stream of camera frames to a camera exclave, which works alongside a person recognition exclave with face and voice recognition models and an identity database. When a person comes into view, the camera exclave detects the person and lets the main OS know that a person may be present, but no image data leaves the Secure Exclave. An audio exclave does the same thing with audio.

The person recognition exclave matches face and voice prints against the identity database of enrolled users, giving a confidence score. The OS gets the person identifier, position, and confidence level, but not any of the actual audio or video. These simple signals are used to activate personal features like Calendar and Messages that depend on identity, with raw sensor data discarded.

Secure Exclaves came about because Apple needed a secure option for ambient video and microphone monitoring, with the groundwork laid starting in iOS 18. Apple devices use indicators for situations where the camera and microphone are actively engaged, but Apple says they weren't ideal for ambient sensing because they would be on all the time. Always-on lights wouldn't give users a way to distinguish between background sensing and active audio and video recording.

There are two modes for a Secure Exclave: ambient mode and active mode. In ambient mode with no indicator, a sensor can respond to triggers, but it only shares small amounts of metadata with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data is given to the operating system, and an indicator informs the user that the system has audio and video access.

Apple has long used indicators, but they are now backed by Secure Exclaves. Secure Exclaves make sure an indicator is active before data is allowed to be transferred from the exclave to the rest of the OS.

title: Nvidia’s CEO scandal could have major repercussions at Apple Park
content:
Macworld





If you haven’t heard, Nvidia is looking for a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang following a scandal involving an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. We won’t get into the particulars (you can read all about it here), but since Nvidia is perhaps the most important chip manufacturer in the world thanks to AI, it’s going to need a new permanent CEO as soon as possible. Among the list of candidates are your typical Nvidia internal executives, as well as several from outside the company.
Here’s why Apple fans should care: Apple’s Chief Hardware Officer Johny Srouji has been named by Bloomberg as a top candidate for Nvidia’s CEO position. Citing Srouji’s leadership of the “most successful in-house silicon programs in the industry,” Bloomberg notes that Srouji’s “track record gives him deep credibility on chip design, product integration and long-term technology roadmaps.”
The list also includes Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, who was named interim CEO following Huang’s resignation, Nvidia VP Ian Buck, AMD CEO Lisa Su, Micron Technology CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, and others. To be clear, these are all major players in the tech world with deep knowledge of the chip industry.
What’s less clear from the report is whether the list of candidates was obtained from an Nvidia source or simply some educated speculation by the Bloomberg reporters, but it makes sense that Srouji would be considered.  A longtime exec and face of Apple’s keynotes, Srouji has led Apple’s chip efforts from the start, including the development of the first A4 chip in the iPhone and M1 chips in Macs. 
Apple’s A-series chips are a major reason why the iPhone continues to be the best-performing smartphone in the industry, and the transition of Mac hardware from Intel chips to Apple silicon has been a huge success that has contributed to the Mac’s growing market share. They continue to set the standard for mobile and desktop processors, and have upended the consumer chip industry as manufacturers scramble to compete.
Srouji was named Apple’s Chief Hardware Officer earlier this year, at the same time Tim Cook announced his retirement as Apple CEO. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in December 2025 that Srouji seriously considered leaving Apple, and the speculation is that the promotion to CHO was part of an effort to keep him at the company. “I don’t plan on leaving anytime soon,” Srouji reportedly said to his staff in response to Gurman’s report. But that was then, and being handed the reins of one of the largest companies in the world could cause him to reconsider.
Less likely to be a candidate is Tim Cook, who stepped down as CEO on September 1. His name wasn’t included in the Bloomberg report but President Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social network that Cook is the “only one man” who could fill Jensen’s shoes as CEO. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote.

title: Mac malware doesn't need a security flaw when users do the work
content:
Bitdefender's latest Mac threat report shows adware gaining ground as attackers increasingly use browser scams to trick users into bypassing Apple's security protections.

MacBook Air M5
Bitdefender's September 2026 macOS Threat Landscape Report analyzes more than 1.5 billion security events collected between August 2025 and July 2026. Excluding web and document threats, adware rose from 22.6% of detections in the previous report to 34.4%.
Trojans remained the largest category at 45.2%, down from 51.8%. Potentially unwanted apps also fell from 25.3% to 20.4%.
The shift reflects the growing prominence of malicious ads, browser redirects, and deceptive software installers that trick users into compromising their Macs.

title: Apple’s rumored smart glasses were just confirmed by a supplier. Whoops!
content:
Macworld





Apple, as a general rule, is extremely secretive about its unreleased products. But that rule doesn’t always apply to its supplier partners, whose PR strategies may not be quite as strict or polished. And sure enough, one of those companies now appears to have revealed, quite blithely and deliberately, the existence of Apple’s rumored smart glasses project.
The Changzhou-based firm Quick Intelligent Equipment this week made its Q3 2026 earnings report. And according to a Chinese-language article by People’s Finance News (via MacRumors), this report contained the explosive claim that the supplier’s revenues were bolstered by working with Apple on a new set of “smart earphones” and a pair of AI glasses. Neither of those projects has yet been announced by Apple, and therefore neither of them has officially existed… until now.
“The company has participated in Apple’s AI glasses and new smart earphone projects, which will help drive related businesses such as precision welding assembly and machine vision inspection,” the report claims (via Google Translate), without appearing to realise how much trouble someone could get in for leaking that information anonymously, let alone publishing it in a public financial disclosure. (Quick Intelligent Equipment didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.)
Granted, Apple itself leaked video of a new set of camera-equipped AirPods this summer, which is likely what the “smart earphones” refers to. But the AI glasses are simultaneously a bigger deal and a better-kept secret, and John Ternus will be very frustrated if a supplier really has spilled the beans in this bizarrely shameless way.
Apple has already entered the mixed-reality wearables business with the Vision Pro, but the company hopes at some point to launch something more portable and appealing to mainstream users. Widely referred to by external media as Apple Glass, and reportedly known at Apple Park by the codename N50, Apple’s first set of smart glasses are expected to be ready for a launch as soon as the first quarter of 2027. We’ll all have to pretend to be surprised.
creator: Macworld

title: Nintendo to End 'Sign in With Apple' Support in January
content:
Nintendo will stop allowing users to sign in to their Nintendo Account with an Apple or Google account on January 26, 2027, the company has announced.


Users will also no longer be able to create a Nintendo Account through either service. Nintendo has not explained why it is removing the options, but notes that the exact cutoff could be delayed depending on the progress of its system updates.

After the change, users will need to sign in with their Nintendo Account email address or Sign-In ID and password, or use a passkey. Nintendo says users who are already signed in on a device may not need to sign in again immediately.

Nintendo Account login page to request a reset email.

Sign in with Apple may have an Apple-generated relay address registered with Nintendo. Messages sent to that address are forwarded to their personal inbox. Nintendo advises anyone who can no longer access their registered email address to contact its support team.

We’ve rounded up the best MagSafe, Qi2, Qi2.2 25W, and MagSafe-compatible magnetic chargers, from the plain pad to multi-functional stands (up to six devices charged), and even the most colorful—from snap-on chargers and modular stands to foldable power banks and full charging desk mats.
Apple’s MagSafe technology, supported by all models of iPhone since the iPhone 12 (except the iPhone SE and 16e), presents a more efficient way of wirelessly charging compatible iPhones. MagSafe is the ring of magnets around the iPhone’s internal charging coil that senses compatible accessories and magnetically snaps securely into the most efficient charging position with the right accessories. With MagSafe, you’re less likely to wake up to find your phone wasn’t correctly placed on the wireless charger so didn’t charge at all!
Testing the best for you
We have tested a lot of magnetic chargers—MagSafe, Qi2 and Compatible—and here inform you which one will work best for you. There are simple magnetic wireless chargers, multi-device chargers for iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods, travel chargers, car chargers and more. 
Best simple MagSafe chargers
Best 2-in-1 MagSafe chargers
Best 3-in-1 MagSafe chargers
Best 4-in-1 MagSafe Chargers
Best travel MagSafe chargers
Best MagSafe charging stands with power banks
Best MagSafe car charger
Best wireless charging desk mat
Best wireless charging sleeve
Offering up to 25W power output in the right configuration, MagSafe charging is much faster than basic 7.5W magnetic wireless charging. The similar magentic Qi2 standard, supported by the iPhone 13-18 families (and unofficially the iPhone 12 but strangely not the latest 16e) offers similar 15W speed charging. Qi 2.2, also known as Qi2 25W, meets MagSafe at 25W for iPhone 16/17/18 series.
MagSafe or Qi2 certification
Apple certifies MagSafe accessories to ensures that the output charging is 15W for most iPhones, and up to 25W for iPhone 16 and later (with Apple’s latest MagSafe charger or chargers certified for Qi2.2 25W). Non-certified magnetic but “MagSafe-compatible” chargers are usually just 7.5W with a ring of magnets to hold your phone in place. Certified MagSafe chargers also have a single-wire NFC antenna that allows the iPhone to identify the device and a built-in magnetometer to prevent compass interference while you are using your iPhone while it’s charging.
In our tests, 15W MagSafe and Qi2 chargers are evenly matched for charging speeds. 7.5W MagSafe compatible chargers, as you might expect, take around twice as long—certainly in the early stages of charging. But don’t rule out 7.5W chargers as they are often high quality, nearly always noticeably cheaper and just take a while longer to fully charge an iPhone. The king of the hill is Apple’s new MagSafe charger and chargers based on the new Qi2.2 25W technology that are definitely faster at 25W, but only with iPhone 16 or later.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Simple vs multi-device magnetic chargers
The most basic form of MagSafe or magnetic charger is the simple pad that latches on to the compatible iPhone. Some pads feature a pop-out arm so the iPhone can be propped up while charging. There are also products that can simultaneously charge an iPhone plus other Apple devices, such as an Apple Watch or wireless AirPods charging case. Note that the AirPods case must be of the wireless variety, and the original 2016-19 AirPods case lacked this functionality. The base of a multi-charger could also be used to charge a second iPhone but mostly not magnetically and at 5W rather than 7.5W, 15W, or 25W. Also see our round up of the Best Apple Watch chargers and stands.
Best simple MagSafe chargers
A simple MagSafe charging pad is the cheapest route to wireless iPhone charging. If you are going to the bother of connecting this product to a wall charger, why not just use a Lightning (iPhone 14 or earlier) or USB-C (iPhone 15 and up) cable direct to the iPhone? You can fast-charge an iPhone to 50% battery in under 30 minutes using a cable and just over that using a 25W charger, while it takes around 45-50 minutes to wirelessly charge iPhone from 0 to 50% using even 15W MagSafe.
That said, there are interesting options to choose from. After these we’ll look at more multi-functional MagSafe chargers.

The most obvious MagSafe Charger to buy for your Apple iPhone is, of course, the Apple MagSafe Charger. It’s the charger that Apple would have shipped with the iPhone if it did such things anymore. It’s as minimalist a design as you’d expect from Apple–it looks a lot like a giant Apple Watch Charger. You can also use it to charge your AirPods.
Apple’s latest version of this charger offers fast 25W charging speed with iPhone 16 and later (15W for older iPhones). It also added a 2-meter length option for $10/£10 more, which is most welcome. At least a 30W USB-C power adapter is required for 25W charging. In our tests using the Apple MagSafe Charger we wirelessly powered up an iPhone 16 Pro from 0% to 50% in just over 30 minutes.
It can also charge your AirPods case (AirPods 2 and later, or AirPods Pro), although not at the same time as the iPhone—for that, you’ll need at least a 2-in-1 wireless charger, see below for options.
The standard 1m cable is too short to comfortably charge and use your iPhone at the same time, or maybe stretch from a power socket to a nearby table, so we recommend the 2m upgrade. Don’t forget that this Apple charger still requires a USB-C power adapter—at least 20W if you want 15W charging and at least 30W to enable 25W charging.

The 25W Belkin UltraCharge Magnetic Charger Pad is now just as fast as Apple’s charger for the iPhone 16/17/18 families, and comes with a long cable and handy pop-up stand. The cable is twice as long as Apple’s basic model, which makes using the phone much easier when charging. It’s also thicker nylon-braided cable with a handy integrated silicone cable tie. The pad itself measures 1.7 x 2.4 x 0.6 inches (43 x 60 x 16mm).
Belkin sells two versions, one with a squarer back shape and one rounder—the difference is minimal. There’s also an option to buy with a 36W power adapter (for a very reasonable extra $10) included or just on its own if you already have a wall charger to use.
Again, a straight cable connection will be faster but we like the kickstand, which you don’t get with a standard cable connection.
There are a few very similar Belkin Charger Pads so make sure you get what you’re after. Wirelessly charging at maximum 25W generates a fair amount of heat that can trigger the iPhone into dialling back the power to defend itself from battery damage. The ESR Cyclone, as its name suggests, aims to tackle this with an active cooling fan (called CryoBoost) and open-duct airflow that should mean it stays closer to its top power output longer than merely passively cooled chargers.

The premium-quality, vegan leather Journey NEXA laptop sleeve bills itself as a “4-in-1”, and it certainly is multi-functional.
As well as protecting your laptop during travel, it includes two wireless chargers (one MagSafe compatible at 7.5W; one 5W for AirPods or a second phone) and can work as both a desk mat and mousepad to free your workspace of clutter.
The most recent NEXA Lift model features an iPhone charger that raises into an adjustable stand.
While it comes with a USB-C cable, you’ll need to add your own charger (check our roundup of the best iPhone chargers) to connect with the USB-C port in the sleeve. Alternatively you can charge the MacBook itself while it sits protected in the sleeve—for this you’ll need a more powerful MacBook charger.
Why wireless?
Wireless charging is convenient and fine for situations when you don’t need a super-fast recharge, although the latest 25W wireless chargers are getting close to the power and therefore speed you’ll get from charging via a cable
If you’re leaving your home in 20 minutes and need as much juice as possible, plug in a cable (USB-C for iPhone 15 or later, or Lightning for earlier iPhones) into a USB-C charger (of at least 30W) to power up an iPhone faster than wireless. With 25W wireless chargers you can simply place your iPhone on and know you should be able to charge it to 50% in around 30 minutes.
Wireless charging is less wearing than constantly inserting a cable into your phone, and more reliable as that vulnerable cable port can fill with fluff and dust after all the time spent in your trouser pocket or bag and it’s one of the most common reasons that an iPhone refuses to charge even when connected with a cable. It’s easy to clean with a toothpick (but please do it softly!) but will affect most of us at some time. Read our tips about how to clear dirt and fluff from your iPhone’s charging port.
Wireless charging isn’t affected by the build-up of dust and fluff in the phone port and is also less vulnerable to oxidation and corrosion.
With wireless, you don’t have to remember to run around trying to find who’s taken your charging cable, and it’s certainly a lot neater.
Of course, wireless charging is not really wireless, unless you are using a portable magnetic power bank. The magnetic charger is still connected by a cable to your wall charger; it’s just the connection to the phone that is properly wireless.
What else you need
Some magnetic chargers come with their own wall charger, but most require you to add your own. Apple recommends at least a 20W USB-C power adapter (wall-socket charger) and we agree unless your charger supports 25W wireless charging, in which case go with at least a 30 USB-C charger or higher if it’s a 2-in-1 or 3-in-1 multi-device charger.

title: Apple Home Collection: Select Accessories Available to Order This Friday
content:
Apple today announced that select Apple Home Collection accessories will be available to order starting Friday, November 13, with availability beginning in December. Apple did not say exactly which accessories can be ordered tomorrow, so stay tuned.


Introduced alongside Apple's new HomeView smart home hub last month, the Apple Home Collection is a new lineup of smart home accessories that LG and Schneider Electric designed in collaboration with Apple. There are indoor and outdoor cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, a video doorbell, and a door lock.


 	
LG Video Doorbell ($249.95) - The Video Doorbell has dual cameras that capture views of visitors and packages. The front camera has a 2.5K resolution and the bottom camera is full HD resolution. It has a built-in spotlight and a chime that plays through HomeView, HomePod, or HomePod mini.

 	
LG Outdoor Cam ($299.95) - The Outdoor Cam has low-light color night vision and can be angled in multiple positions.

 	
LG Indoor Cam ($199.95) - The Indoor Cam has a privacy-preserving feature that allows it to tilt up when people are in the home so it's not recording, and down when people leave for keeping an eye on the home. The tilt function works based on geofencing, but can also be controlled in the Home app or manually.

 	
LG Floodlight Cam ($399.95) - The Floodlight Cam has dual floodlights that activate when motion is detected and low-light color night vision.

 	
LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($349.95) - The lock has Ultra Wideband and can unlock automatically when the homeowner approaches, with no tap required. It also supports unlocking via PIN or a hidden backup key slot, and there is detection for whether the door is opened, closed, or has been tampered with. The doorbell and lock can work together as one, letting users see who is at the door and unlocking it if needed.

 	
LG Thermostat ($199.95) - The thermostat supports Adaptive Temperature and in the U.S., heating and cooling can be activated during lower-cost periods for users with a compatible utility plan. The thermostat can read temperature and humidity across multiple rooms using separate temperature and humidity sensors. Sensors are priced at $39.95.

 	
Schneider Electric Thermostat ($199.95) - Also supports Adaptive Temperature and can be used with temperature and humidity sensors. Sensors are priced at $39.95.

For more details about the accessories, read our previous coverage.

title: Apple Says HomeView Software Update Coming Next Month With Siri Fix
content:
In her HomeView review shared in a free edition of her New Things newsletter today, tech journalist Joanna Stern said Siri AI once told her "I don't have a camera to see you," even though the device has a camera. Apple confirmed to Stern that it plans to release a software update in December with a fix for this issue.


Siri AI also refused to open Stern's garage door or unlock her front door, even though the HomeView recognized her. Apple told her that the software update coming next month will enable this functionality. In the meantime, you can unlock door locks and garage doors by opening the Home app on the HomeView and tapping on-screen controls.



"Today users recognized by HomeView can unlock security accessories, including door locks and garage doors, directly on their HomeView screen," an Apple spokesperson told Stern. "With a software update next month, this will extend to Siri AI, giving users more ways to manage security accessories once they've been recognized."

title: Apple’s Black Friday Deal 2026: What to expect from its shopping event
content:
Macworld





The biggest shopping day of the year is Black Friday, which this year falls on Friday, November 27, 2026. If you are looking to buy an Apple product then Black Friday is a good time to buy. Apple typically runs a Black Friday-to-Cyber Monday shopping event.
The company usually offers gift cards with eligible purchases rather than lowering Apple Store prices. We don’t yet have details of Apple’s offer for 2026, but Apple’s 2025 promotion was announced on November 20, so this year we expect an announcement on or around Thursday, November 19. 
In 2025 Apple offered gift cards worth $25 to $250 in the U.S. (£20 to £200 in the U.K.), depending on the eligible product – including a $75 gift voucher with an iPhone 16, $100 with an iPad Air, and up to $250 with a MacBook Pro; third-party retailers, such as Amazon and Best Buy often provide direct discounts instead. Apple also offers education pricing, refurbished products, and trade-in credit.
For the latest discounts from other retailers, see our roundup of the best Black Friday Apple deals.


When will Apple announce its Black Friday 2026 offer? 
Apple’s 2025 promotion was announced on November 20, so this year we expect an announcement on or around Thursday, November 19.
The event is likely to run from November 27–30, if Apple follows its usual pattern. 
Once the deal is live you will be able to see details here:
 Get Apple's Black Friday offer (U.S.)
 Get Apple's Black Friday offer (U.K.)


							


Does Apple do a Black Friday sale?
Does Apple hold a Black Friday sale? We wish it would but, unfortunately, Apple’s Black Friday offer is usually a giveaway of Apple Gift Cards with certain purchases made during the Black Friday period. It gives away gift cards with select purchases from Black Friday to Cyber Monday each year, we expect it will do the same between November 27 and November 30 2026.
In 2025, the company gave away up to $250/£200 with Macs, $100/£80 with iPads and $75/£60 with iPhones. This was a better offer than in November 2024 when the company gave away gift cards with values up to $200/£160 with select purchases made in the Apple Store (online and in person) on Black Friday, as well as on the Saturday, Sunday and on Cyber Monday. You can see how much Apple gave away in 2025 compared to what it gave away in 2024, 2023 and 2022 below.
Apple often excludes recently launched products, although there are exceptions: Apple Watch Series 11 and AirPods Pro 3 qualified in 2025. That makes some of this fall’s launches less likely candidates for the 2026 promotion, but no eligible products or exclusions have been confirmed.


						

							


Is Apple’s Black Friday offer worth waiting for?
Apple usually gives gift cards with selected purchases rather than lowering prices, so waiting for Apple itself may not get you a cheaper price. Black Friday is often one of the strongest periods for Apple deals, though discounts can also appear through November, Prime Day and other sales. Consider an early offer if it is close to that model’s previous low; stock and popular configurations can run out, and the biggest reductions often apply to older or clearance models. 
In short: Compare retailer discounts with the value of Apple’s gift card before deciding. Treat the card as its full face value only if it covers spending you already planned, and compare the exact same model and configuration.


						

							


What was Apple’s Black Friday offer in 2025?

Apple’s Black Friday deal 2025 vs 2024

The 2025 promotion also included some recent launches: Apple Watch Series 11, Apple Watch SE 3, and AirPods Pro 3 each came with a $50/£40 gift card, despite arriving just a few months earlier.  FAQ 


1.
When do the Black Friday sales begin? 
Black Friday officially begins on the day after Thanksgiving, which in 2026 is Friday, November 27. However, the sales begin well before that–we saw deals starting at the beginning of November. The main event runs through the weekend and concludes on Cyber Monday, which is November 30.





2.
Should I wait for Cyber Monday to purchase?
While it’s always possible that a better deal is waiting around the corner, if you see a good deal, don’t wait. While Cyber Monday promises impressive deals there’s always the risk that the Apple device you want sells out and you miss out on the great deal everyone else got.





3.
Are Apple’s Black Friday gift cards worth it?
Apple’s gift-card offers give you extra value on an eligible purchase rather than an immediate price cut.
A key benefit is flexibility: you can put the card toward another Apple product or services and digital purchases, such as subscriptions and App Store purchases.
That flexibility is most valuable if you expect to spend more with Apple. A gift card doesn’t lower the price you pay for the qualifying item, and it may be less appealing if you don’t plan to buy anything else from Apple; competing retailers may offer direct discounts instead.





4.
Can I use the gift card toward the product I’m buying?
No. The gift card can only be used for future purchases. 





5.
What can I buy with an Apple Gift Card?
An Apple Gift Card is remarkably versatile – it can be used to buy almost anything Apple sells, including hardware, services, subscriptions, and digital content.
This means you can use the balance toward:
Physical Apple products: iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, AirPods, HomePods, Apple TV, and accessories like the Apple Pencil or Magic Keyboard .
Apple services and subscriptions: Apple Music, Apple TV+, iCloud storage, Apple Arcade, and Apple News+ .
Digital content: movies, music, games, apps, and in-app purchases from the App Store, iTunes Store, and Apple Books
The card can be redeemed to your Apple Account, and the balance never expires . It’s accepted at the Apple Store (online and in retail locations), the App Store, and across Apple’s digital storefronts.





6.

title: How to stop your MacBook sleeping when the lid is closed
content:
Macworld





Many Mac users want to turn their MacBook into a desktop-style workstation, using an external display, keyboard, and mouse with the lid closed – a setup often called clamshell mode.
Running a MacBook this way can make sense for several reasons, from supporting multiple external monitors on certain Apple-silicon models to freeing up desk space and improving ergonomics. Others may want their Mac to keep working with the lid closed while it downloads files, runs backups, plays music, or so you can keep your AI agents running.
The problem is that macOS is designed to put a MacBook to sleep as soon as you close the lid. Apple does support clamshell mode (or closed-display mode), which lets you use a MacBook like a desktop by connecting an external display, keyboard, and mouse while the lid is closed. However, this setup comes with strict requirements: clamshell mode won’t work without an external monitor, and it can introduce performance or thermal trade-offs. If those limitations don’t suit your needs, there are alternative approaches – including third-party apps and system settings – that can keep a Mac awake with the lid closed. Just ensure that if your Mac is running in clamshell mode you do not put it inside a bag or enclosed space as it is likely to get hot. 
In this article we cover: What you need to use a MacBook with the lid closed, the steps to follow to use a MacBook with the lid closed, different methods to stop a Mac sleeping when the lid is closed, how to play music or continue a download while a MacBook lid is closed, and how to wake a MacBook with the lid closed.


Why would you want to use a MacBook with the lid closed?

				
					

				
			
Using a MacBook with the lid closed. 

Petter Ahrnstedt




There are several functional and technical reasons why you might choose to operate your MacBook with the lid closed.
Save desk space
Connecting an external display, keyboard and mouse lets you use your MacBook as a desktop computer. Closing the lid frees up space, particularly if you use a suitable vertical stand, while a larger monitor can provide a more comfortable working setup. Keep the Mac’s ventilation openings clear.
Keep tasks running
You may want downloads, backups, music playback or other tasks to continue while the lid is closed. A supported external-display setup keeps the Mac usable with the lid shut. Without an external display, you’ll generally need a utility that specifically supports closed-display operation, as explained below. Keep the Mac stationary and ventilated while it works; don’t put it in a bag.
Use multiple monitors
Multiple monitors give you more room to work and let you keep several apps visible without constantly switching between windows. You could write a document on one screen while consulting research on another, or keep email and chat separate from your main workspace. Closing your MacBook’s lid lets you work entirely on external monitors while freeing up desk space.
External display support depends on the chip. Base M4, M5 and M6 MacBook Pro models, plus M4 and M5 MacBook Air models, support two external displays. M5 Pro supports three; M1 Pro through M4 Pro support two; and M1 Max through M5 Max support four. Closing the lid doesn’t increase these limits.
Base M3 models support two external displays only with the lid closed, requiring Sonoma 14.3 or later on the Air and 14.6 or later on the Pro. Opening the lid disconnects the second monitor.
Base M1 and M2 MacBooks support one external display, although DisplayLink accessories and software offer a workaround. Resolution and refresh-rate limits vary; check individual specifications, particularly for Intel models.
See also: Best stands for MacBook and Best MacBook docking stations. 


						

							


Why does my MacBook sleep when I close the lid?
Apple doesn’t officially support disabling sleep when the lid is closed without an external monitor and power source by default, but there are workarounds. 
MacBooks are designed to enter a sleep state when the lid is closed primarily to manage power consumption and protect the hardware. This automatic transition helps preserve battery life and prevents the device from overheating while stored in a confined space like a backpack.
The reasons for this behavior include:
Power Management: Closing the lid triggers a standby mode that significantly reduces power usage.
Hardware Protection: If a MacBook remains active while closed in a bag, it can overheat and become really hot because it is still processing tasks without adequate ventilation.
Automatic Updates: While asleep, macOS may occasionally wake the system to install updates or sync data, though this can sometimes lead to the device becoming unexpectedly warm if it doesn’t return to sleep properly.


						

							


What do I need to use a MacBook with the lid closed: Clamshell Mode

				
					

				
			You’ll need an external monitor (or two), a mouse and keyboard to use a MacBook with the lid closed. 
Foundry




To operate your MacBook with the lid closed, you must have specific external hardware connected and meet the following requirements:
Power Source: Apple’s recommended setup for using a MacBook in closed-display (clamshell) mode is to connect an external display, a power adapter, and an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad. While some newer MacBook models — particularly Apple Silicon systems — may continue to operate with the lid closed while running on battery power, this behaviour can vary depending on the Mac model, macOS version, and connected peripherals. For the most reliable and fully supported clamshell-mode experience, Apple recommends keeping the MacBook connected to power.
External Display: The Mac must be connected to an external monitor.
External Peripherals: You must have an external keyboard and mouse (wired or Bluetooth) to wake and control the computer.
Up-to-date software: Using a MacBook with the lid closed is a lot simpler than it used to be if you are using a newer Mac and a newer version of the Mac operating system. In fact, if you are experiencing issues using your Mac with the lid closed then it is likely that you could address this by updating your Mac to a recent version of macOS, assuming your Mac supports it (see our macOS compatibility checker).  Newer versions of macOS have made this process much smoother, resolving many of the bugs that plagued older Intel-based MacBooks.


						

							


How to use a MacBook with the lid closed
Follow these steps to use your laptop as a desktop computer by connecting it to external peripherals while the built-in display is shut.
Connect your MacBook to power. Use its charger, or a compatible USB-C monitor or dock that supplies power to the Mac.
With the lid open, connect your external display, keyboard and mouse or trackpad. If you use Bluetooth peripherals, make sure they are paired with your Mac.
Turn on and unlock your MacBook. On Apple silicon models, click Allow if macOS asks permission for a connected accessory to connect.
Wait until your Mac’s desktop appears on the external display, then close the lid.
The external display may briefly go dark. If your desktop doesn’t reappear, press a key on the external keyboard or click the mouse to wake the Mac.
You can read more about using a second display with your Mac here.
But even with these settings, if you aren’t attached to an external monitor closing the lid will cause the Mac to sleep.
What if you don’t want to plug in an external display? Read on… 


						

							


How to stop a MacBook from sleeping when the lid is closed 
Suppose you don’t want your MacBook to sleep when you close the lid? Maybe it is busy downloading something and you don’t want it to stop. Or maybe you’ve left it downloading an update overnight or syncing your Time Machine backup, and you’d prefer not to see the backlit keyboard. In another scenario you might want to play music from the MacBook without having to have the lid open – something likely to appeal to a few DJs.
The problem is that your Mac will go to sleep when you close the lid if it’s not plugged in and connected to an external display.
To stop a MacBook from sleeping when the lid is closed – specifically when it is running on battery power and not connected to an external monitor – you generally need to use third-party software or advanced system commands. By default, macOS is designed to enter sleep mode in this state to preserve battery life and prevent overheating.


						

							


Option 1: Use a Third-Party App like Amphetamine
A utility that supports closed-display operation can keep your MacBook awake with its lid closed. Our recommendation is Amphetamine, which is free and can be downloaded from the Mac App Store:
As noted in our round up of the best free Mac apps, Amphetamine will keep your Mac awake. Featuring a menu bar-based interface, the app lets you temporarily override your Mac’s sleep schedule (even when your MacBook’s lid is closed) and even adds a few useful features like activating only when connected to specific Wi-Fi networks and keeping only certain drives awake.
Free at  Mac App Store						
					
To configure Amphetamine for this specific scenario, follow these steps:
Download and open Amphetamine (it’s on the Mac App Store).
Click the pill-shaped icon in your menu bar
Select Quick Settings.
In the Session Defaults section, uncheck the box for “Allow system sleep when display is closed”.
Start a new session using “Indefinitely” or “While File is Downloading” or “While App is Running”) to keep the Mac awake after closing the lid.
Your Mac may need to be plugged in while the download continues. 
On Apple silicon MacBooks, connecting or disconnecting external power can affect Amphetamine’s closed-display sessions. The developer offers an optional Power Protect helper to address this behavior. Follow the guidance presented by the app, and check that your session continues after closing the lid or changing power sources.
Alternatively, Caffeinated is a paid app available on the Mac App Store here for $3.99/£4.49. Version 3.2 introduced an option to keep your MacBook awake with the lid closed. Enable its closed-lid option for this purpose.


						

							


Option 2: Use a dongle
You can use a dummy display plug that tricks your MacBook into thinking it’s connected to an external display, thus putting your MacBook in clamshell mode and keeping it running.
You can find a four-pack of UGreen HDMI dummy adapters on Amazon for nine bucks.


						

							


Option 3: Use Terminal Commands
If you prefer not to install third-party software, you can use the Terminal to disable sleep mode entirely.
Open Terminal. 
Enter the following command: sudo pmset -a disablesleep 1
That should stop your Mac sleeping. 
Please note that using this command will prevent the Mac from sleeping in all scenarios until you reverse it by entering: 
sudo pmset -a disablesleep 0


						

							


Can Battery settings keep a MacBook awake with the lid closed?
In System Settings > Battery > Options, “Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter when the display is off” keeps your plugged-in Mac awake when its screen turns off. 
However, this setting alone does not override sleep triggered by closing the lid. 
For closed-lid use, follow the external-display setup above or use a utility that specifically supports closed-display operation.


						

							


How to play music with your Mac’s lid closed
You can use the free Amphetamine app (mentioned above) to keep your Mac awake while the display is closed, here’s how:
Once installed on a Mac you will find a pill-shaped icon in the menu bar at the top of the screen. You can choose from options such as Start New Session While File is Downloading or While App is Running.
If you want to keep Music (or what app you are using) running with the lid closed, first, you need to have that app open. Then follow these steps:
Click on the Amphetamine icon in the menu bar.
Click on Quick Settings.
In the Session Defaults section, deselect “Allow system sleep when display is closed.”
Go back to the main menu and select While App is Running and pick Music or the app you are using. If your app is not open, it will not appear in the list. Only apps that are running appear.
You will now be able to shut your Mac’s lid and continue listening to Music. 

				
					

				
			
Foundry



							


How to continue a download with a MacBook lid closed

				
					

				
			
Foundry




By default, macOS puts your MacBook to sleep when you close the lid. In sleep mode, most apps stop running, which means regular downloads in Safari, Chrome, Steam, or other apps will usually pause.
To keep downloads running with the lid closed, you need to prevent your Mac from fully sleeping.
Your best option is to use a third-party app, like Amphetamine. Follow the steps in the section above and start a session by selecting While File is Downloading or While App is Running (select your browser or download manager).
“Wake for network access,” found in System Settings > Battery > Options, allows your Mac to wake briefly so other users can access shared services. It does not keep the Mac continuously awake or override sleep when you close the lid. Don’t rely on it to keep browser or game downloads running; those require the Mac to remain awake.
With a utility such as Amphetamine preventing sleep the following downloads can continue: 
browser downloads
cloud storage syncs
Steam/game downloads
large file transfers and uploads


						

							


How to wake a MacBook with the lid closed

				
					

				
			You can use a Mac while it’s closed.

Halyna Kubiv




If your MacBook is asleep, you can usually wake it without opening the lid when it is connected to an external display, power, and an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad.
Make sure the external display is switched on and the MacBook is receiving power.
Press a key on the external keyboard or click the mouse or trackpad.
If the Mac doesn’t wake, open the lid and check its power, display and accessory connections.
These steps wake a sleeping MacBook. If it has been shut down, open the lid and press the power button if it doesn’t start automatically.
For scheduled startup and wake-up, see our separate guide to scheduling your Mac to turn on and off. If FileVault is enabled, you must log in after startup.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Can a MacBook run with the lid closed without an external monitor?
By default, a MacBook is designed to enter sleep mode as soon as the lid is closed to preserve battery life and prevent overheating. Apple does support a closed-display mode (aka clamshell mode), but with hardware requirements that typically include an external monitor. However, there is third-party software, such as Amphetamine, that will allow you to override the default sleep schedule, keeping the system active even when the lid is shut and no external display is present.  





2.
Is it safe to stop a MacBook sleeping with the lid closed?
Yes. Apple supports using a MacBook with its lid closed when connected to an external display and accessories. Keep it on a hard, flat surface with ventilation openings unobstructed, and never leave it running inside a bag.
Thermal performance depends on the model and workload, though. Geekerwan, as reported by Macworld, found a closed-lid cooling advantage for the PROLED XDR MacBook Pro over the older mini-LED model tested.





3.
Why does my external monitor turn off when I close my MacBook?
If the external display goes dark when you close the lid, check that your MacBook is receiving power, the display is connected correctly, and an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad are available. A compatible USB-C display or dock may supply power without a separate charger. 
On Apple silicon models, open the lid and unlock the Mac to approve connected accessories if prompted. Then close the lid and try waking it with the external keyboard or mouse.





4.
Can I use clamshell mode on battery power instead of plugging in the charger?
In some cases, yes. Certain newer MacBook models – particularly Apple Silicon models – may continue to operate in clamshell mode while running on battery power. However, Apple’s recommended and officially supported setup for closed-display includes connecting the MacBook to a power adapter. 
Behaviour on battery power can vary depending on the Mac model, macOS version, and connected peripherals, so using external power is the most reliable configuration for clamshell mode.





5.
What’s the difference between sleep mode, clamshell mode, and preventing sleep on a MacBook?
The primary difference between these modes lies in how the MacBook manages its power, display, and background tasks when the lid is closed.
Sleep Mode: Sleep mode is the default state for a MacBook when the lid is closed. In this state, the system pauses most operations to conserve battery life.
Clamshell Mode: This mode allows you to use your MacBook as a desktop workstation while the lid is closed. This mode is officially supported by Apple but requires specific external hardware to function, including an external display, a power source, and external peripherals like a keyboard and mouse. 
Preventing Sleep: In some cases you might want to keep a MacBook fully active even when the lid is closed, without necessarily meeting the strict hardware requirements of clamshell mode. Since macOS doesn’t support this you need a third-party app, or you could plug in a dongle that makes your Mac think you have a display plugged in.

title: HomeView is Apple’s first post-iPhone device
content:
Macworld





On November 13, Apple will finally start shipping its long-awaited HomeView smart home hub. While the leaks gave us an early look at some of its specs, the official launch exposed its underlying philosophy through distinct hardware and software choices. Although the HomeView is unmistakably designed for iPhone users, its unique direction ushers in an all-new product type built for a future when Apple’s iconic handset doesn’t exist.
New yet familiar
The iPhone is by far Apple’s most influential product, and it will likely remain so for a very long time. Because of that legacy, every major Apple device released since its debut has felt like an iteration of the iPhone in one way or another—tweaked to accommodate a specific purpose. For example, many users continue to perceive the iPad as a large-canvas iPhone, while the Apple Watch essentially doubles as a mini iPhone strapped to your wrist. The Vision Pro similarly follows this direction, sharing familiar UIs, the App Store, and common Apple feature sets, acting as an advanced spatial iDevice of sorts. Even the MacBook now has a Dynamic Island.
We’ve reached a point where most of us are surrounded by screens all day long. Whether we’re working during daylight hours or winding down in the evening, chances are we’re facing some kind of rectangular display. Many of us now live in digital bubbles, privately consuming online content and increasingly detaching from our real-life surroundings. Apple’s HomeView doesn’t contribute to the rampant isolation; it discourages it and breaks the longstanding cycle.

				
					

				
			
Apple’s HomeView ad was an exaggerated view of a family’s frenetic morning routine—but no one was using an iPhone.

Apple




If you’ve seen Apple’s frenetic ad, you noticed that the featured family was using the HomeView in tandem. The home hub harmoniously switched between different user profiles and executed all kinds of tasks in an open, social manner. They could all tell what each member was generally up to based on their voice commands, but private details like iMessages remained solely visible to the active user.
Unlike the Apple TV 4K, the HomeView isn’t designed for long usage sessions. While it supports video streaming, it’s the first Apple product to offer an awkward 7-inch square screen, making it impractical for media consumption and other immersive experiences. It’s meant to keep you present in the moment with other household members around you.
Early preview
The HomeView expectedly borrows app icons and other features from the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, but it doesn’t behave like any traditional Apple device.
The original iPhone did not offer an App Store and instead limited its users to the core apps included at launch. Likewise, it took the Apple Watch years to support untethered apps and provide a dedicated App Store on watchOS. That, however, does not mean that the HomeView will ultimately follow suit and introduce an App Store. After all, the smart home hub has reportedly been ready for around two years and was only held back due to Siri AI’s delayed release. Apple had plenty of time to port its digital storefront’s foundation to the new platform, but it made a conscious decision to maintain the virtual shackles.
Opening the floodgates would bridge the gap between the HomeView and iPad, which would defeat its whole purpose. Apple doesn’t want the HomeView to become your next TikTok doom-scroll destination. And barring third-party smart home management apps that encourage users to invest in its HomeKit ecosystem—reinforcing its walled garden further.

				
					

				
			
HomeView bridges the screen in your pocket and the people in your house.

Foundry




A Siri-centric future
HomeView’s support for CarPlay extensions and App Intents in compatible iPhone apps via Siri AI suggests that the App Store’s omission is a deliberate move to also push third-party developers to fully adopt App Intents in their software. Otherwise, users likely won’t be able to easily interact with their apps using the smart home hub.
As more developers build for Siri AI and its reliability improves, users will have fewer reasons to pick up their iPhones. They’ll be able to conveniently communicate with others, adjust plans, and make reservations by simply talking to the tiny display in the center of the room. Apple could also potentially minimize the reliance on nearby iPhones by indexing data stored in iCloud, which includes messages, emails, events, reminders, notes, photos, files, and much more. Gemini can already tap into Google Workspace data from any device, and Apple could realistically build a similar infrastructure down the road.
By the time Apple’s rumored smart glasses and other AI gadgets debut, presumably enough developers will have embraced App Intents and Siri AI, all thanks to the HomeView. This will make these fresh concepts—which will primarily operate with Siri’s assistance—fully functional and practical from day one, increasing their popularity and appeal among consumers. Despite beating with an iPhone’s A18 heart, the HomeView is secretly architecting a world where the iPhone stays in our pocket—or perhaps doesn’t exist at all.

title: Apple Support Community Deserved a Proper Goodbye
content:
Apple on Tuesday abruptly placed the Apple Support Community into a read-only state and announced that the forums will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20. Those who contributed to the site — some for more than two decades — were blindsided by this decision and had no chance to post farewell messages.


Even if you felt the Apple Support Community contained too many generic or unhelpful answers from users trying to boost their post counts and earn points, the people volunteering their time to the site still deserved a proper goodbye.

Below, we have highlighted some of those people and their experiences.

Jeff Donald from Florida was a member of the Apple Support Community since November 2000, when the forums were still known as Apple Discussions. This past year, Apple recognized his efforts by inviting him to the Apple Community+ program, which launched in 2022 and provided members with a few extra perks and experiences.

Leroy Douglas was a member since July 2009. He said he was a bit shocked to see Apple's sudden announcement, but he saw the writing on the wall.

Tobias Steen in Germany said there were also Apple Support Communities in Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. For some reason, the French and German versions do not have closure notices, but we are told they will meet the same fate.

Evan Bato Rousseau in France to 83-year-old Nobel Prize winner Sir Tim Hunt in England, who told us he found it to be a helpful resource, even if some of the answers were wonky.

John Daniel, the Canadian developer of macOS diagnostic tool EtreCheck, said he was active in the Apple Support Community for more than two decades. Users like him who reached "Level 6" or higher based on their contributions received access to The Lounge, a private category of forums where Apple employees sometimes participated.

Prior to 2020, John said Apple occasionally hosted in-person meetups for Support Community members, including a special visit to Apple Park. 

"I don't agree with comments that so many are making about the Apple Support Community right now," he said, in response to those who described it as useless. "We regularly solved problems, identified significant issues with Apple projects, traced the cause of bugs and fixed them, and always learned new things. That's what I'm going to miss."

Elías Rojano Núñez of Chile participated in the Spanish forums. He told us that he found it deeply satisfying when he was able to help others, and he was saddened that the Spanish forums were shuttered without any advanced notice, but he is grateful for the opportunity that he had and will always value the interactions he had with fellow contributors.

Rojano Núñez shared a photo of some of the items he received from Apple over the years, including a 5-year Apple Support Community anniversary pin. There were also 10-year, 15-year, and 20-year pins. Over the years, merchandise given out included Apple-branded hats, shirts, tote bags, and even umbrellas once.


Whatever its shortcomings, the Apple Support Community was more than just a place to ask questions. For some, it was a place to belong.

good riddance.
This article, "Apple Support Community Deserved a Proper Goodbye" first appeared on MacRumors.com

The Duo joins the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, although limited launch stock means getting Apple’s first foldable could require patience. Meanwhile, there are some excellent U.K. deals on the discontinued iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max as retailers clear remaining stock. If you want premium cameras and performance without paying the latest Pro prices, those older models are worth considering.
Apple rarely discounts its newest iPhones directly, and its 2026 price increases have made choosing carefully even more important. Black Friday may bring better offers, particularly through carriers and trade-in promotions, but a strong discount on the right phone can make buying now worthwhile.
In this guide, we explain whether now is a good time to buy each iPhone, which models are worth waiting for, and when to expect the best deals. We’ll help you weigh the appeal of Apple’s newest hardware against the savings available on older models.

The worst time to buy an iPhone
This is generally in the weeks leading up to Apple’s September launch event, or in the early spring, when new models are expected to be announced. Buying just before a refresh means you could miss out on new features or pay full price for a model that’s about to be superseded.
The best time to buy an iPhone 
This depends on where you live:
In the U.K., where most iPhones are sold unlocked and off contract, the biggest savings are typically available during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day (usually in July and October, and occasionally in March) and Black Friday in late November. However, worthwhile iPhone discounts can be found throughout the year if you know where to look.
In the U.S., where people tend to buy iPhones through a carrier, the best time to upgrade is often during Black Friday when networks enhance their offers with larger trade-in values, bill credits, gift cards, or discounted service plans. 
Due to the Black Friday sales, November and December could be a particularly good time to grab a deal on an older iPhone, such as the iPhone 17 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro Max. 


						

							







Should you buy a new iPhone now or wait? 
Wait for Black Friday, November 27, 2026.  

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




September and the months that follow are a much better time to buy an iPhone than earlier in the summer (July and August are usually poor months to buy a Pro iPhone because Apple’s September launch is so close). The iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo have now been unveiled, removing that uncertainty.
If you need a phone now, there’s little reason to wait for another annual refresh, and the iPhone 17, 17e and Air are also relatively safe purchases because their successors aren’t expected until spring 2027. See: iPhone 18 and 18e rumors and iPhone Air 2 rumors. 
The iPhone 17 remains the strongest value, with a 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage for $899/£899 (although it was previously $799/£799). The 18 Pro and Pro Max make more sense if you want the best cameras, performance or battery life, while the Duo is for buyers specifically interested in Apple’s new folding design.
There is, however, one important reason to wait: 2027 could bring a much bigger iPhone redesign. Apple is rumored to be preparing a 20th-anniversary iPhone – the iPhone 19 or 20 with a near-all-screen curved design, under-display Face ID, possible solid-state buttons, a thinner and more efficient OLED display, a larger battery and major camera improvements. That could make 2027 a more significant upgrade year than 2026.
So if your current iPhone is still serving you well, waiting could be worthwhile. If you need a phone now, wait until Black Friday if price is your main concern.

Should you wait for the iPhone 18?
For most people, there isn’t a strong reason to wait for the iPhone 18. Apple isn’t expected to launch the standard model until spring 2027, so buying an iPhone 17 before the end of 2026 would still give you several months with Apple’s current mainstream model before its replacement arrives.
The iPhone 18 is expected to bring a 2nm A20 chip, potentially 9GB or 12GB of RAM, Apple’s C2 modem and possibly a new 24MP front camera. Extra RAM could prove particularly useful for future Apple Intelligence and Siri features. However, the rear camera system is still expected to consist of two 48MP cameras, while the display may remain broadly similar to the iPhone 17’s 6.3-inch ProMotion panel.
There is also some uncertainty over exactly what the iPhone 18 lineup will look like. A September 2026 rumour suggested Apple could effectively merge the standard iPhone and iPhone Air into a single model, rather than continuing them as two separate devices. If that happens, the iPhone 18 could adopt some of the Air’s thinner, lighter design while retaining the broader appeal of the standard iPhone. For now, though, that remains speculative.
Price is another consideration. With the arrival of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, Apple increased iPhone prices across the range, so the iPhone 17 now costs $899, $100 more than at launch. When the iPhone 18 arrives, it is likely to inherit that $899 price point, while the iPhone 17 could drop back to around $799 at which you may regret buying it at the higher price.
Wait if you want the newer A20 chip, potentially more RAM, an improved front camera, or are intrigued by the possibility of a thinner redesigned standard model. 
Don’t wait if you simply want ProMotion, dual 48MP cameras, excellent battery life and 256GB of storage as standard – the iPhone 17 already delivers all of that.
